Additional findings relate to vectorial Boolean mappings and their non-linearity.

A popular method of compactly representing binary arrays of a specified width and height is through constant-margin binary arrays, which consist of a series of horizontal and vertical line segments that bound the array. A more efficient way to store and work with these arrays is to select a smaller yet equivalent subset of these line segments. The challenge is to reduce the number of selected lines while ensuring that the reduced representation accurately captures the original binary array. The optimal number of lines for this reduced representation is known to be within a specific range of the array's size, but the exact minimum number it can reach is unknown. A more precise estimate of this minimum number is achieved by taking the ceiling of a specific number that represents how full the array is with the original set of lines. A more accurate calculation of this fullness measure is also achieved.

I propose a theoretical framework for PDF adjustments that incorporates the effects of heavy flavors within a theoretical context. This involves using PDFs to model parton distribution functions, and then utilizing a theoretical correction to account for the effects of heavy flavors in QCD. This correction can be applied using various methods, such as next-to-leading-order calculations or higher-order approximations like asymptotic free parts. A novel approach to PDF adjustments is also presented, one that utilizes a reweighting technique based on next-to-leading-color contributions and is accompanied by a theoretical uncertainty estimate.

This document presents an ongoing evaluation methodology that facilitates a comprehensive assessment of various clustering algorithms. To achieve this, we leverage the ELKI data mining framework, which offers a diverse range of evaluation metrics. By integrating our methodology into the framework, we gain the ability to apply multiple evaluation methods to various datasets, thereby gaining insights into their comparative performance. Currently, our repository comprises 148 evaluation methods, which we make publicly available alongside the paper. 

The ELKI framework itself boasts an impressive collection of mining tasks, including clustering, classification, association rule discovery, and outlier detection, among others. Developed with the aim of promoting transparency in data mining operations, the framework demonstrates our research goals and is designed for public use. As a result, the framework has served as a tool for comparative evaluations in previous studies. 

In this study, we detail our evaluation approach, highlight the features of the framework, and present the results of our comprehensive experiment, which evaluates clustering algorithms on 289 datasets using 114 different evaluation methods. 

The ELKI framework is openly sourced at https://elki-project.github.io/blog/index.html and can be downloaded at https://sourceforge.net/projects/elki/.

We've developed an innovative technique for seeding a range of optical frequencies from a single master laser. Our method, known as parametric sowing, utilizes a nonlinear microresonator to produce a frequency-locked grid of over 100 lasers with a low addition energy per laser, and maintains stable lockover a long period of time. Our theoretical model reveals that to achieve stable locking, the line width of each laser within the grid must be lower than a specific threshold, and our experimental findings align with this prediction.

We establish that in any acylindrically hyperbolic group, a subgroup generated by loyal elements, which stabilize a fixed subgraph, constitutes a finite stochastic group. This finding is built upon several key conclusions, including a demonstration that a loyal subgroup's intersection with a finitely generated subgroup is also stochastic, as well as a proof that the intersection of two stochastic subgroups is both finite and stochastic. Additionally, we define and investigate a certain type of stochastic subgroup known as a 'loyal invariant stochastic subgroup', developing a series of properties and relationships for such groups. It is shown that a loyal invariant stochastic subgroup of an acylindrically hyperbolic group is equivalent to a subgroup of its commutator subgroup, formed by a specific mapping of generators. This relationship is further utilized to establish connections between the conjugacy classes of such subgroups and combinatorial properties of graphs, including forest-like structures and planar graphs. This work further speculates on the potential relationships between these groups, independence from other existing theories, and the potential generalization of these groups to broader mathematical structures.

Quantization has significant benefits of reduced storage and processing requirements for neural networks, which can also improve classification robustness to adversarial attacks. There's an underlying connection between quantization and the non-convex nature of the loss surface, which explains its positive effect on generalization. This relationship is examined through the lens of the neural tangent kernel (NTK) regime, which treats NNs as Riemannian geometries with a unique loss surface landscape. Since binary weights can be viewed as realizing the eigen-decomposition of the NTK, we investigate binary weight neural architectures, analyzing how quantization affects the eigenvalues and facilitating generalization analysis. These findings are validated by experimental results on various datasets, which also demonstrate that binary weight neural networks outperform their full-precision counterparts.

We introduce the quantum extreme surface as a generalization of the quantum minimal surface. This surface defines a one-dimensional subspace associated with specific bulk-boundary correspondence. By examining the quantum extreme surface, we can gain insights into the structure of the holographic entropy. Specifically, we demonstrate that the quantum extreme surface is linked to a particular direction in the boundary direction set, which enables us to characterize its properties. Furthermore, we derive a mathematical expression for the norm of the Riemannian volume form on this surface. This allows us to clarify the relationship between geometric and spectral contributions to the holographic entropy. Moreover, we investigate how the quantum extreme surface evolves in time following an initial excitation. This analytical study enhances our understanding of the quantum extreme surface and the quantum minimal surface, which are fundamental concepts in holographic quantum mechanics.

Research into discrete systems using a lattice structure has been enhanced by a novel intersection multiplicity formula applicable to various combinatorial models. This formula has been independently verified using both algebraic and combinatorial approaches. By extending previous work on lattice paths, the formula has been modified to account for more complex scenarios, including models affected by a variable parameter. The resulting theorem can be applied to multiple situations, such as finding patterns in Sullivant's semigroup and analyzing models of self-interacting particles.

Signal reconstruction techniques like iterative soft-thresholding or iterative hard-thresholding can effectively recover sparse signals from compressed sensing measurements. However, these methods may diverge or converge slowly without or with regularization, respectively. To stabilize these iterations, different approaches can be taken. In this study, we introduce and examine several stabilization methods for these iterations, including those based on momentum-like updates and orthogonal projections. A key boundary case involves Clèment's iteration, which corresponds to an under-determined system with a non-unique solution. To recover the signal, we propose a suite of stabilization methods for this iteration as well. To assess our methods, we use a compressed sensing test signal and benchmark against alternative approaches.

We have derived expressions for the point spread functions of combined images in terms of their individual beam weights, which are applicable to a wide range of imaging situations, including single data and data sets from interferometry. The PSFs of combined images are found to be dependent on the orientation, but unless there is significant weight disparity between beams, the positional shift is minimal. The Stokes map of an image is calculated by combining the weighted Stokes maps of each individual beam, and the peak normalization of the combined image's PSF is determined by the sum of the squared weights of each beam. The calculated weights are often optimized to minimize the weight sum of two data sets in interferometry, and the determined PSFs show self-symmetry around the phase center, with the combined image of two data sets exhibiting a slightly shifted position that increases with the magnitude of weight differences.

Gaussian free field correlations that are confined to a domain or an interface drive related stochastic processes such as SLE and serve as critical elements in constructing log-distributed random matrices. These fields, defined on a planar domain bounded by a simple curve, have local derivatives that follow a specific distribution, specifically Gaussian with zero mean and a specific variance. The derivative's sign and magnitude can be considered as propagating a local 'charge' along the boundary, resulting in distinctive field patterns based on the charged points' distribution. We've established a link between these fields and multiple SLE processes, each driven by a distinct log-gas, or matrix. The specific distribution of the field's local derivatives determines the desired SLE process, effectively propagating a specific 'defect' along a complex boundary. These findings have significant implications in understanding statistical behaviors of both random matrices and fractal domains.

This research demonstrates that for the Cauchy problem of the Navier-Stokes equations in multiple dimensions, there are no general theoretical guarantees of existence and uniqueness for periods exceeding a certain critical time, $T_{adj}$, which serves as an upper limit. However, we successfully derive a novel inequality that estimates the solution's error, $v$, in terms of the initial data's error, $u_0 - v_0$, with a dependence on the nonlinearity constant and the Laplacian's inverse, but independent of the higher derivatives of $u_0$ and $v_0$. This breakthrough allows us to make definitive predictions about the behavior of certain infinite sequences related to the nonlinearity's extreme value, which were previously unknown. Moreover, in the case of periodic data, we establish that the $L^2$ norm of the velocity field's derivative is bounded in the time interval $[0, T_{adj}]$, but fails to do so in the larger time interval $[0, +\infty)$. In addition, we investigate the "blow-up" scenarios, considering both the scenario where the initial data is smooth and that of highly irregular data, and demonstrate the occurrence of "blow-up" in the latter case.

The explosion of data necessitates an urgent need for innovative techniques that can swiftly validate the results of quantum computations. As a significant breakthrough, our study demonstrates the potential for a significant reduction in the time required for validation, specifically from quadratic to linear duration, using a traditional approach on randomly generated data. This breakthrough is attributed to the application of a conventional, widely accepted method - the Lanczos tridiagonalization technique. Our research employs 48-core processors and showcases that this approach can successfully execute validation tasks on large-scale datasets, yielding a substantial speedup of nearly 20 times. Additionally, our study reveals that these results can be accurately replicated using a smaller, optimized dataset that requires minimal core counts, thereby paving the way for the development of compact, portable validation benchmarks.

Cells in a developing embryo undergo a intricate process where they divide and differentiate into specific forms. Researchers have created computer models to simulate this process, but accurately representing the complex shapes of cells in these models is a challenging task. Most current methods use surface-based representations which require explicit definition of cell boundaries, but this can be difficult when dealing with irregular or hard-to-define shapes like those found in actual cell images. A new, more flexible method uses implicit neural networks to represent cell shapes in a learning-based approach. By training a neural network to predict the probability of a point being inside a cell based on its coordinates, this method can generate a 2D map of a cell's shape. When combined with a generative model, this map can be used to generate new, simulated cell shapes. We evaluate this method's effectiveness by comparing its performance to other shape representation methods, and find that it can generate realistic cell shapes and even predict unknown areas of cells. It has the potential to advance the simulation of cellular processes and the prediction of cell behavior in development and disease.

Our study explores how spatial memory is represented in the brain by training rats using a reversible inactivation technique and subsequent retrieval tests of spatial reference memory. Two key findings emerge from our investigation: Firstly, the strategy employed by the rats to navigate space is more intricate than initially suggested, involving not just one, but multiple mental map representations of space. Secondly, specific brain regions, such as the hippocampus, play a more dynamic role in learning and adaptation than previously believed, with their functions shifting between encoding and retrieving spatial information.

Researchers examined a two-dimensional system composed of rigid disks with varying masses that interact with each other and an external magnetic field, resulting in unique magnetic properties. Due to the lack of a detailed balance in this system, it cannot be efficiently sampled using traditional Monte Carlo methods based on reversible Markov processes. However, a novel method was developed to correctly sample this system by mapping it onto a reversible Markov process. Additionally, two alternative approaches were proposed to tackle even more complex systems, including those with inhomogeneous magnetic fields and flexible disks. Simulations demonstrated a high level of agreement between the new method and existing techniques.

The challenge of localizing multiple sound sources and categorizing their types is addressed in the 2019 Sound Event Detection and Localization Task held at DCASE. Our submission for this task uses a method that involves training a Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network with a specific filter size, demonstrating the effectiveness of this design in pinpointing sound sources. Additionally, we enhance our results by applying data enhancement that involves channel rotation, and by taking into account the spatial arrangement of audio signals. On a Sound Event Detection and Localization baseline system, our findings show significant enhancements through this method.

Concurrent transmission based wireless systems hold promise for enhanced data rates and efficiency in emerging applications. Superposition transmission (ST) stands out as a promising technique with significant potential for improvement in existing systems. However, research on ST is largely fragmented, making it essential to synthesize current knowledge and identify areas for further exploration. This paper offers a comprehensive overview of ST in wireless communication systems, covering fundamental concepts, performance assessment methods, performance bounds, and available literature, as well as highlighting potential research avenues and applications. Furthermore, we address critical challenges such as optimizing ST strategies, designing efficient detection techniques, and addressing statistical issues related to ST.

Consider a discrete-time, complex-valued system output $y[n]$, influenced by a complex-valued input $x[n]$, and a complex-valued impulse response $h[n]$, with additive complex-valued noise $w[n]$. Given a relatively short signal duration $N$, we want to estimate the system $h[n]$ that produced the observed output $y[n] = s(h)[n] + w[n]$. Since the noise $w[n]$ masks the system output to a significant degree, directly estimating the system $h[n]$ using traditional methods isn't effective. Nonetheless, collecting numerous realizations of $y[n]$ allows us to obtain reliable insights into the underlying system, as our research utilizes random matrix theory to investigate the statistical properties of this real-level data collected through spectrogram mappings. Our investigation exposes inherent connections linking the system $h[n]$ to characteristics present in the covariance matrix of its real-level data. We develop a novel approach to estimate the system $h[n]$ by determining the spectral density of its real-level data, as well as the system matrix $h[n]$, which is shown to converge consistently when the number of realizations increases infinitely. Additionally, our method is capable of providing a partial system estimation even when the number of realizations is less than the system length $h[n]$. Our study supports these claims with theoretical proofs and corroborates them with numerous experimental examples.

In a community of interconnected agents generating random walks with two possible outcomes, we examine the dynamics of a spiking neural network using a mean-field description. We observe two distinct states: one where a significant portion of agents converge on one outcome, and another where these agents evenly split between the two options. When the system transitions between these states, it exhibits features reminiscent of chaotic systems, including irregular patterns and a high degree of statistical unpredictability. However, unlike typical chaotic systems, this regime is only fully utilized when the system lies at the equilibrium of two competing states. Through detailed analysis and extensive numerical studies, we propose a universal method to detect this regime by monitoring the relationship between two statistically independent quantities, and provide concrete examples of how this approach can be applied in both small and large network models.

One approach to stimulating orbital chaos in $N$-body problems is to utilize randomized forces as a diagnostic tool for identifying unstable regions in a simulation. Here, an implementation of this idea is integrated into the REBOUND code and tested with a simple two-body system, then a more complex setup involving three bodies, with positive results.

In various physiological processes, the body regulates its internal balance through feedback mechanisms to maintain homeostasis. We have developed a mathematical framework, modeled after Albert Einstein's 1905 paper on Brownian motion, to analyze these regulatory responses. We apply this framework to study the interactions between the pancreas and insulin-producing cells, specifically how the pancreas adjusts its insulin release in response to the cells' insulin sensitivity levels. We derive a quantum-like stochastic equation, known as the quantum Fokker-Planck equation, to characterize the system's dynamics and determine that the system follows a stationary distribution known as the Cauchy distribution. We validate our findings by comparing them with existing research and observations on glucose regulation.

Two-dimensional flows past grouped obstacles arranged in an alternating sequence are analyzed. The obstacles are represented as circular discs with varying radii, confined to a single file in a channel, and the study assumes no obstruction when the flow rates exceed a certain threshold. The calculated flow rates are validated numerically using both finite element methods and a Lattice Boltzmann approach. Based on an extended parametric study, an empirical formula for the flow resistance is developed. This study also compares the flow patterns around grouped obstacles in an alternating sequence with those around uniformly grouped obstacles.

Research has shown that the El Ni\~no-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) significantly affects the global climate, particularly in areas experiencing unusual precipitation patterns. ENSO's impact on regions with very low and elevated seasonal precipitation behaviors remains less understood. By analyzing unique ENSO patterns extracted from climate simulations with various levels of ENSO amplification, this study identifies new ENSO variety types and their distribution patterns around the world. We find that these new ENSO patterns emerge due to changes in spatial patterns during the wet and dry seasons, resulting in distinct temporal evolution patterns. We name two ENSO variety types: 'delayed mature phase' and 'early mature phase', characterized by distinct phases. Analysis of precipitation patterns reveals that these new ENSO patterns are associated with precipitation changes in parts of South America, Africa, Australia, and the western Pacific. We develop a statistical framework that selects the most likely ENSO variety type based on precipitation pattern similarities. Notably, this study discovers that the 'delayed mature phase' ENSO variety type is associated with low precipitation levels in northeastern Australia and the surrounding regions, while the 'early mature phase' ENSO variety type is associated with low precipitation levels in southwestern Australia and the surrounding areas. These findings demonstrate that unique ENSO patterns can produce distinct climate responses in the Southern Ocean and Australia by influencing the spatial and temporal evolution of ENSO.

A long-standing mystery in the field of massive black holes persists. It involves understanding the seeds of these massive black holes that reside at the centers of various galaxies, including small dwarf galaxies like Leo I. Theoretical models suggest that either massive stars or alternative theories such as primordial black holes could act as the seeds. The latter option is considered unlikely but offers a natural candidate for resolving the 'compactness problem' associated with heavy star formation. Recent observations of a compact, ultra-dense core in the galaxy Leo I support the possibility that primordial black holes could have formed there. This observation uses the relationship between a galaxy's core density and the age of its stellar population to determine the upper limit of the efficiency of heavy star formation. The observed upper limit is lower than what is typically found in similar galaxies, indicating a very low rate of heavy star formation in the core of Leo I and suggesting that primordial black holes could be the dominant component of the galaxy's central core. This possibility is not ruled out by any other observation and therefore remains an intriguing hypothesis that needs to be explored further.

In this study, we explored the transport and Correlation effects in a model multi-orbital Kagome alloy, specifically $Cr_2Sn$_-1$x$As$_2$. Our findings, derived from specific heat, magnetization, resistivity, and Hall coefficient measurements, reveal the presence of a flat band induced adverse magnetoresistance at low temperatures. X-ray diffraction analysis confirmed that our sample single crystal exhibits a trigonal structure with the $P\bar{3}m1$ space group. With increasing x values, our Hall coefficient exhibited an intriguing non-monotonic change, possibly influenced by changes in electron correlation and band structure. Additionally, we observed flat band induced adverse magnetoresistance, characterized by a sharp decrease in resistivity below 30 K for x = 0.5. For x = 0.75, however, we saw a normal decrease in resistivity below 20 K. Our observations of Correlation-enhanced negative magnetoresistance further validated this phenomenon.

The uncovering of the human genome has marked the beginning of a new era in science and medicine.  Although significant breakthroughs have been achieved, many of the genome's secrets remain unsolved.  To effectively interpret genomic data and draw conclusive findings from large-scale association studies, international cooperation and data sharing among researchers are essential.  A collaborative exchange of information allowed for the discovery of new genetic variations associated with traits such as human height and body mass index, which had gone undetected through individual analyses.  Additionally, this exchange enabled the examination of how these variations affect gene expression and helped to clarify the underlying mechanisms behind many unresolved genome mysteries.

Researchers have been studying the residual kernels of block configurations in designs, which has led to a current investigation on groups that can create such kernels through a single action on a set of blocks. It is demonstrated in this paper that for a specific type of block configuration, a particular group that can create this configuration when acting on a set of blocks, also has the ability to create an equivalent configuration when acting on a block for each orbit under a given group action. Additionally, it is shown that for a specific case of block configurations, a particular group action results in unique orbits of blocks and points, demonstrating the maximal possible group action in this scenario.

The behavior of entropes derived from Hugenholtz-Van Hove variational theory is analyzed for confined hydrogen-, helium- and lithium-like ions in their ground states. It's clear that as the ionic number increases, the influence of Coulomb interaction does the same. This phenomenon is true whether the interaction is within the electrons themselves or between an electron and a nucleus. Additionally, for fixed ionic number, increasing the confinement strength leads to greater Coulomb interaction. This trend is also seen when switching from hydrogen to helium and then to lithium ions. It's noteworthy that the entropes evaluated with Hugenholtz-Van Hove theory can serve as reliable indicators of Coulomb interaction strength.

A variety of methods have been utilized to test how gravity affects the motion of binary stars, with some methods revealing deviations from the standard gravitational model and assigning a deviation parameter $\gamma$. This study employs a novel approach by comparing observed data on binary stars from the Hipparcos catalog with simulated data generated under the standard gravitational model. This method allows for a more straightforward comparison with other tests of gravity and does not involve complex calculations. Furthermore, this approach can be expanded to utilize a wider range of observations without requiring the acquisition of additional data. Based on a preliminary analysis, no significant limitations are imposed on the value of $\gamma$, with an estimated uncertainty of $10^{-4}$ au$^3$ d$^{-1}$.

In the course of proving the soundness and completeness of a structural proof theory for multiplicative linear logic with an emphasis on proof transformation, two key concepts are clarified. Firstly, there's a clear definition of when a proof can be eliminated, encompassing both atomic and composite units. Secondly, there's a defined method for cutting a proof while retaining its validity, applicable to both atomic and composite units. These concepts are then utilized to establish lemmas concerning the manipulation of proofs under certain structural changes. Furthermore, by establishing that every proof can be reduced to a product-free form, we gain insight into the inherent complexity of proof validation in this context.

Interpreting and comparing the behavior of complex time series, such as those found in financial markets, is a challenging task due to their intricate patterns and the lack of clear causality. Traditional methods like cross-correlation often fall short, providing only a partial understanding of these sequences. A more effective approach involves analyzing the temporal relationships within each time series, either by incorporating the history of observations or through the use of cross-recurrence plots, which can also be used to develop predictive models for sequence behavior. A novel method utilizes cross-recurrence plots to categorize time sequences into different groups based on their similarity of behavior, with potential applications including portfolio management and risk assessment. A significant finding emerges from the analysis - it becomes possible to forecast whether a given time sequence will synchronize with a reference sequence at a specified time, indicating a significant advancement in understanding and controlling the behavior of complex time sequences.

We investigate how temporary distortions of a quantum system affect its electronic and magnetic properties by using a formalism that accounts for dynamic vibrations. We derive equations for electronic and magnetic self-energies that are influenced by molecular or atomic vibrations. We apply this framework to study a paradigmatic model system, specifically a tight-binding model coupled with an harmonic oscillator. We examine the impact of electron-phonon and spin-phonon interactions on related materials and calculate their respective self-energy and transport properties. We demonstrate that by incorporating a momentum-dependent vibration, we can generate a significant and adjustable interaction between electrons and molecular vibrations, thereby creating new phenomena. Additionally, we investigate the charge density and transport properties of a model system with vibrating sublattices and obtain results that indicate that dynamic vibrations can serve as a mechanism for controlling these properties. We also observe that under certain conditions, we can generate a significant and adjustable doping-driven interaction between electrons and molecular vibrations. Lastly, we find that by varying the frequency and amplitude of molecular vibrations, we can generate low-energy excitations that are sensitive to these variations, thereby providing an explanatory framework for several observed phenomena in materials with dynamic vibrations.

To boost sales, companies frequently run promotions, but accurately forecasting their effectiveness is challenging. Current methods leverage historical user behavior and advertising content, yet often fall short due to the limitations of relying solely on numerical representations of content. In contrast, our proposed approach, PromoteVision, incorporates visual promotion data into the forecasting process by employing a network to differentiate between promising and underperforming ads, based on their visual characteristics. In contrast to existing methods, PromoteVision integrates both numerical user behavior and visual promotion data, using a unified model to forecast promotional effectiveness, thus enabling more informed decision-making. In our evaluation, this approach outperformed leading industry benchmarks, achieving a 5.8% relative improvement in forecasting accuracy, thus demonstrating its ability to provide more precise predictions.

Traditionally, business process management employs entity relationship diagrams and Unified Modeling Language (UML) class diagrams to model data structures. However, these tools fall short in their ability to restrict attribute relationships effectively, leading to incomplete and potentially inaccurate models. This shortfall is addressed by a proprietary technique called data constraint modeling, which offers a unified framework for business data representation and constraint definition. This technical document presents a specific data constraint modeling method focused on limiting attribute relationships, with examples demonstrating its application. Furthermore, the document considers issues in validating the method, including consistency between constraints and their effectiveness in data structure limitation, as well as strategies for checking constraint compatibility.

Wildfires disrupting solar energy significantly through atmospheric aerosols,
resulting in economic losses for industries that operate in the solar energy sector.
To improve forecasting, there is a pressing need for more accurate representations
of wildfire aerosol behavior. To address this, we develop a novel deep learning model
that incorporates physical principles and utilizes multiple satellite sources for forecasting
solar radiation. By utilizing wildfire aerosol behavior as a learned representation,
our model effectively incorporates this information into the forecasting. In addition,
our model's ability to learn from diverse satellite sources enhances wildfire aerosol
characterization, even in areas with limited satellite coverage. When tested, our
model demonstrated improved wildfire aerosol forecasting and solar radiation predictions
in the San Francisco area during the 2020 wildfire season.

For a stationary location tracking system, we investigate the disclosure of user location information to a flexible type of query while maintaining privacy. Users submit queries in the form of conditional expectations, and we analyze the optimal strategy for the server to respond with relevant location information while minimizing the user's revealed location details. We establish a method for the server to achieve the best trade-off between transparency and user anonymity by strategically releasing location distances or areas, and provide computational implementations to demonstrate the efficiency of our framework. Furthermore, we explore how users can adjust their query to achieve desired levels of privacy. Our model encompasses a wide range of location tracking systems including $k$-anonymity and $\epsilon$-differential privacy.

Research has shown that estimated connectomes derived from resting-state fMRI are unreliable on an individual basis, yet are finding their way into clinical practices and risk assessment tools, which raise important ethical concerns. To address these issues, we suggest adopting a data-driven, probabilistic approach to quantifying and comparing connectivity strengths between groups. This approach uses empirical distributions of group-derived connectivity patterns to define statistically significant differences and claims. Furthermore, our methodology enables accurate prediction of behavioral and clinical traits from brain connectivity, while maintaining control over type I errors and ensuring the generalizability of the findings. This goal is achieved through Bayesian modeling and inference techniques. We illustrate the effectiveness of our proposed methods in rfxml by example analyses of publicly available and open-access resting-state fMRI datasets.

Inspired by the Francis and Carne theorem, we take a directed graph as a complex that applies diffusion and a modified Dirichlet form. This allows us to establish a connection between the thermal resistance and the negative sectional curvature within each directed loop. Furthermore, we demonstrate that at thermodynamic equilibrium, the density of an arbitrary energy function is directly proportional to the Dirac operator's spectral count. This relationship holds under the condition that the negative sectional curvature within each directed loop is consistently over a certain threshold, but remains unclear in counterexamples such as the hypercube and the ladder.

In recent years, research on code-mixed language models has gained significant traction, driven by the growing accessibility of data in this language format, particularly on social media platforms. Code-mixed models leverage symbols from multiple parent languages to express one expression with multiple languages. This paper introduces a novel approach to tackling the language modeling challenge posed by code-mixing. Our proposed model, PESTO, dynamicly identifies critical language shift points and employs relative positionality to incorporate contextual context, yielding better performance than existing methods when tested on the languages employed in Wikipedia entries.

Using a quasi-two-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model with two equivalent directions, we investigate how isotopic mass replacement and pressure affect the critical temperature of the hypothetical p-type H3S superconductor at varying pressures. Around 4-50 GPa, we find that the critical temperature follows a simple scaling law with mass replacement, but this simplicity is challenged when the isotopic mass ratio exceeds a certain threshold, causing a nonlinear relationship with pressure. Additionally, we identify the influence of the Fermi velocity's anisotropy on this critical temperature, and explain that phenomenon using a simplified model near a singular point in the Fermi surface. This singularity significantly affects the critical temperature, resulting in a nonuniform change with pressure, and potentially limiting the simplicity of superconducting properties in H3S. Based on our findings, we suggest several experiments to verify these predictions, and explore alternative methods to confirm or refute these results.

Fisher left an enduring legacy in the field of genetics, and his theory continues to be relevant today, with the average effect of a gene's influence being a particularly significant concept in modern analysis methods. We will demonstrate how this average effect plays a crucial role in establishing causality in the field. To begin with, we define a statistical model that allows genes to affect phenotypes directly or indirectly. Next, we formulate principles for a valid causal interpretation of the average effect. We then develop mathematical criteria to determine whether this average effect can serve as a reliable measure of a gene's influence. Under certain conditions, we found that the average effect accurately represents a gene's influence if it is not influenced by nearby genes. We also discovered that the average effect retains its causal significance even when a gene's action is subject to random variation. To illustrate the practical applications of our findings, we conducted simulations using data from mice, studying a trait controlled by multiple genes with complex interactions. Our results reveal that the average effect provides a reliable measure of a gene's influence, even when the data is limited and prone to measurement errors.

Central to many theoretical and practical applications of legged locomotion are energy-efficient gaits of walking, running, and other movements assisted by active propulsion. However, creating autonomous bipedal robots that can push off from the ground using their feet poses significant control challenges due to the non-intuitive interaction between foot motion, ground reaction forces, and movement dynamics. To develop more robust robotic locomotion systems, we're working on integrating legged movement patterns that incorporate successful push-off behaviors. This integration, which incorporates bipedal walking and running patterns, is being integrated into a robot designed to walk on two legs. Using computer simulations and real-world testing, we've established a relationship between ground reaction forces, foot kinematics, and robot movement. Additionally, we've developed models to predict when and how hard the robot should push off from the ground and to correct any deviations from these predictions. This research is contributing to the development of more resilient robotic locomotion through better understanding and control of push-off behaviors.

Achieving visual relocalization in partially observable environments relies on precise geometric and photometric alignment. Despite effective pre-training methods, deep networks often fall short in diverse environments, necessitating supplemental structures. This research introduces a two-and-a-half-dimensional surfel map framework to aid visual relocalization. The surfel map, comprised of key 3D points, trajectories, and corresponding images, enables robust localization and mapping. The concurrent 2.5D structure facilitates learning of robust features from images, complementing existing deep networks. The integration of these maps greatly enhances both relocalization and navigation accuracy, surpassing current standards. Notably, the proposed map enables accurate relocalization without reliance on prior GPS information or wireless connectivity.

Mobile devices can learn from labeled data, but model ambiguity remains, 
making users unsure which class to choose for an unknown image. We've found 
that, post-federated learning, models often misclassify simple images and 
discard useful data. To address this, we propose a new technique called 
'Ambiguity Reduction for Customized Federated Semi-Supervised Learning', which 
minimizes model uncertainty and increases participation. We've developed a 
new ambiguity measurement method using deep neural network dropout and 
uncertainty estimation, then created an optimized strategy to select the 
most confident participants and engage others with higher ambiguity levels. 
We've tested our technique in a clothing classification task and found it 
clearly surpasses current models in both accuracy and participant utilization.

Simulations of colliding a black hole with a neutron star have been conducted, examining diverse configurations and equations of state for the neutron star. These collisions result in massive tidal disruptions, producing massive accretion disks and powerful jets that are heavily influenced by the neutron star's initial orientation and the strength of any initial magnetic fields in the vicinity. Variations in neutron star equations of state and the colliding geometry lead to significant variations in the mass of the remnants and the disks formed. Notably, when the neutron star maintains a crust composed of neutrons, a substantial mass of matter is accreted onto the black hole, whereas in cases with softer equations of state and inclined collisions, a larger mass of matter is ejected into space. Additionally, in collisions with aligned black holes and magnetic fields, a larger mass of matter is accreted onto the black hole, particularly if a neutron star with a softer equation of state is involved. These findings have important implications for the understanding of gravitational wave observations and the light signals from short gamma-ray bursts.

A curled invariant of a compact Riemannian manifold is defined by an expression involving a curvature operator and the vector fields representing isometrical shifts. This curled invariant exhibits variation across different manifolds, much like the scalar curvature does. Specifically, it takes on a constant value of zero on manifolds featuring special structures, such as hyperbolic ones, and it increases without limit on those with positive Ricci curvature. Furthermore, the relationship between this curled invariant and the scalar curvature, coupled with previous research on lower bounds for the scalar curvature, allows researchers to derive lower bounds for the curled invariant. A notable consequence of this is that any sequence of manifolds with bounded scalar curvature and curled invariant will have a subsequence with uniform sectional curvature that converges to a manifold with positive Ricci curvature.

In a Bayesian setting with limited information, posterior mean estimators may not be unique or may not exist at all. As an alternative, the Q-procedure offers a way to choose an estimator from a family of posterior expectations. While it's known that the Q-procedure converges to the Bayes estimator in various situations, its behavior when there's limited information is not well understood. We investigate what happens when the amount of information available increases and show that, under certain conditions, the probability of significant deviations from the Bayes estimator decays rapidly. We also establish that the expected difference between the Q-procedure estimator and the Bayes estimator converges to zero at a quadratic rate as the amount of information grows. Our study employs a combination of classical asymptotic theory and techniques from high-dimensional statistics.

A novel concept is introduced for creating ultra-bright, tightly focused, and directionally controllable optical fields, harnessing the resonance of surface plasmons on graphene. By positioning a single nanoparticle at the node of an oscillating electric field generated by graphene, we achieve coherent scattering of THz pulses and engineer localized optical fields with unparalleled intensity and spatial precision. Computational models and experimental findings demonstrate the capability to produce customized electric field configurations, offering a revolutionary approach to manipulating matter at the nanoscale and breaking current limits in laser-induced materials modification.

To address the pressing issue of overcrowding in emergency departments (EDs), we developed an analytical framework and numerical tools to model patient arrivals and treatments as a Markov process. Our methodology utilizes Lebesgue-Young measures to define a set of 'typical' reaction curves for treatment durations based on the theory of Mackey and Boyd. Our method extracts a group of non-degenerate reaction curves representative of typical reactions, differing from the extreme cases of almost constant or rapidly increasing treatment durations. These curves provide valuable insights into the dynamics of the ED system and help us quantify the time required for an escape from a crowded ED situation. Our study uses real data from the ED of a major university hospital in France to illustrate the efficacy of this analytical approach.

A novel approach to long-duration missions is proposed, focusing on the collaborative planning and execution of tasks by multiple robots with limited capabilities. Key aspects of this strategy involve each robot utilizing available local information to make independent decisions on which pre-defined global tasks to participate in, and then selecting a specific task to work on. To achieve this, a common global task set is defined and distributed to all robots via a limited bandwidth connection, followed by each robot generating a local list of preferred tasks based on computing power and other resource constraints. A robot then decides which global tasks it has access to and can afford to participate in, and selects one to execute. Through this process, it is demonstrated that a stable equilibrium is reached where no robot wants to change their chosen task list, and a related algorithm performs well in simulation. It is also shown that the overall system performance approaches optimal as the availability of local information and computing power increase. Key benefits of this strategy include reduced communication load and task execution variability. It is estimated that widespread use of cooperating robots could lead to a 5 to 10 times increase in applicable mission durations due to reduced resource usage.

The ALICE Collaboration has investigated the impact of the local parity-odd local charge-dependent two-particle correlation in Pb-Pb collisions at 2.76 and 5.02 TeV. These correlations were analyzed within a specific reference frame known as the Chiral Magnetic Framework. A specific correlation, CMW, was found to be sensitive to chiral magnetic effects, whereas CW correlations were influenced by chiral fermentation and geometric effects. Both CMW and CW influences on CMI were assessed, resulting in predominant limitations of CMI effects observed. Further, interactions between CMI and charge-dependent two-particle correlations, such as CW in hadron-hadron interactions, were examined and constraints on their respective intensities were established. These results could contribute to a deeper understanding of CMI within a certain theoretical framework known as the Chiral Magnetic Framework.

In the context of online fundraising, successfully completing a campaign depends on various crowd indicators, such as social connections and engagement metrics. Research has shown that certain platform-specific features can affect fundraising outcomes, but little is known about how specific crowd indicators impact success when compared across different platforms. Our study aimed to fill this knowledge gap by analyzing data from both crowdfunding and donation-based fundraising campaigns, conducted an experimental cross-platform examination, and identified key indicators linked to campaign success. Our analysis revealed that a strong network, as measured by social connections, is crucial for both crowdfunding and donation-based fundraising, while engagement metrics, such as comments and likes, also played a significant role in donation-based fundraising. These findings provide essential insights for fundraisers and donors, highlighting the importance of leveraging crowd indicators to enhance fundraising efforts, particularly on the donation-based platform, Quỹ.

Cybersecurity threats are continually evolving, leading to increasingly complex and sophisticated cyber attacks that necessitate a highly specialized and adaptive approach to detection and prevention. Research in this area has highlighted the significance of innovative methods in this domain, with a particular emphasis on the utility of machine learning and artificial intelligence. This research paper presents a collaborative cyber threat intelligence exchange framework that employs a novel, federated learning training method to detect security threats. The proposed approach recognizes the importance of real-world, relevant data in training effective machine learning models but acknowledges the constraints associated with data collection and sharing. This study demonstrates that federated learning can be employed to combine datasets for training without necessitating data exchange, using only minor adjustments to existing models. The developed framework involves a collaborative training process where participating institutions contribute to a global model without sharing their individual datasets. This is achieved by initially localizing model training using only a single sample from each participant's dataset, with subsequent iterations refining the global model based on new samples. The exchange of these samples and model updates enables all parties to benefit from the improved collaborative model without requiring data exchange. This research paper showcases the efficacy of the proposed collaborative cyber threat intelligence exchange framework, using network breach datasets as a test case. The results indicate that the federated approach can detect breaches with accuracy comparable to that of a single, extensively available dataset.

A clustering method is developed to improve the ordering of tasks for multi-arm automation. By grouping tasks geographically, the technique reduces the complexity of robot movement and task assignment. A novel algorithm is presented to create these task clusters, minimizing the overall cost of robot movements between tasks. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through simulations showing a significant reduction in robot travel time.

A new set of silicon MOSFETs called SiMOSFETs are made using a standard CMOS process and have a high-carrier concentration in the channel, typically on the order of 1e19 cm^-3. To enable current gain, the channel material is composed of heavily doped polycrystalline silicon capped with a thin, highly n-type or p-type epi-layer. To improve performance, a novel process modification has been implemented to reduce the channel resistance and increase the mobility of the channel material. Using advanced characterization techniques, a record-breaking peak mobility of 700 cm^2/Vs was achieved for both n-type and p-type SiMOSFETs. As a result, a significant reduction in gate resistance and a high switching speed were achieved, with an improved transit time under 10 ns for both transistor types. Furthermore, a high current density of 10 A/cm^2 was maintained while preserving a low voltage, demonstrating the potential for these transistors to replace traditional MOSFETs in high-power electronic systems.

In a diverse group of individuals, optimal performance is often achieved when team members work in sync with each other. Research has demonstrated that in a synchronous team, errors tend to be lower and members tend to perform similarly. While a high degree of synchrony is beneficial, it is usually impossible to achieve perfect agreement due to differences in member abilities or strategies. However, when team members are interconnected through a well-structured network, it is possible to develop a theoretical framework for understanding and predicting how their collective behavior will unfold. Such a framework was established using a 2009 neuroscientific finding that teams following a nonlinear dynamics pattern, characterized by a positive real eigenvalue, tend to converge towards a stable state. Building on this, the present study generalizes this idea to teams following a variety of dynamic patterns and provides a clearer explanation of how intra-group connections affect team performance under these dynamics. Using a theoretical approach, the study evaluates and compares the effects of various team connection structures in achieving low error rates, including the benefits of regular team interactions and the risks of fragmented or overlapping teams. These predictions are validated through simulations based on the widely accepted CKP model.

The effectiveness of information systems can be evaluated based on several criteria, including user satisfaction, completeness of findings, convenience of use, and total interaction time.  A virtual interface can facilitate observations of users without interfering with real system interactions.  However, the present research delves into a uncommon challenge of assessing a source of variation in search outcomes using user testing.  A hypothesis was developed stating that differences in how users browse a video library would affect the quality of their search experience.  A user study comparing two navigation methods, including a basic interface with categories and an alternative with an additional virtual agent interface, revealed significant differences in interaction times and user satisfaction levels.  While both groups showed comparable completeness of findings, the presence of a virtual agent led to a notable 35% decrease in overall interaction time and a 65% decrease in users selecting the basic interface.

In a systematic investigation of monodromy anomalies, we demonstrate that bootstrapping techniques can effectively be applied to a supersymmetric Wess-Zumino model featuring two fermions. By integrating in the conformal bootstrap spirit the asymptotic two-point functions of the twisted sector operators, we specifically derive a function representing the monodromy structure. We find that this function is divisible by an invariant, specifically $I_4(x)$, and that its resulting quotient exhibits the monodromy anomaly. We further verify that our findings align with the predictions of perturbation theory, and that a novel, non-zero anomaly emerges at the third order of the $\epsilon$ expansion.

We find examples of elliptic surfaces, defined over cubic cyclotomic fields, with a point of Shaft height 13. This is in line with the conjecture that minimal height points will appear on such surfaces.

In densely deployed Wireless Local Area Networks, implementing a Medium Access Control protocol that efficiently manages interference relationships is a necessity.
We've developed a new protocol framework, "Stochastic Medium Access using Interference Correlation", which creates a stochastic correlation between nodes' transmission durations and spatial spacing to minimize overall transmission interference.
We've also designed two protocols, "Spatial Stochastic Access" and "Temporal Stochastic Access", which utilize different types of diversity to optimize performance while achieving stable coexistence in WLANS.
Notably, while Spatial StST Access achieves lower packet error rates and similar throughput to Temporal StST Access, it exhibits reduced fairness, showcasing the trade-offs possible through diversity exploitation.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown remarkable performance in node classification, but their reliance on labeled nodes for training can be costly. Pseudo-labeling, a popular semi-supervised learning approach for generating labels on unlabeled data during training, has been applied to GNNs, though its efficacy is hindered by inaccurate pseudo-labels and the challenges posed by domain shift. Our method addresses these issues by introducing an accurate pseudo-labeling technique for GNNs that utilizes semi-self-supervised pseudo-tagging to refine pseudo-labels, leveraging node connections and topological characteristics to identify reliable unlabeled nodes serving as references. These reference nodes are used to assess the validity of pseudo-labels generated during training, enabling the removal of inaccurate ones and resulting in more precise pseudo-labels. Our approach is demonstrated to be effective across various GNN architectures and graph datasets, outperforming traditional pseudo-labeling in accuracy and training time.

In the field of computer vision, creating rich, generalized, and efficient image templates is crucial for a wide range of applications, including semantic image segmentation, object detection, and image compression. Traditional approaches rely heavily on pre-defined classes and are often confined to specific domains, making them less effective in applications involving more complex scenarios, like video processing. To overcome these limitations, a novel deep learning-based method, patch-based template network (PatchNet), is developed, allowing the creation of diverse templates from raw data, even without prior classification information. By iteratively constructing and refining local template patches, PatchNet achieves significant performance gains, particularly in video applications, where the continuous and coherent progression of template patches serves as a powerful image representation. To facilitate seamless image transformation, PatchNet is equipped with a patch shuffling mechanism. When applied to the task of semantic image segmentation in videos, PatchNet delivers impressive results, surpassing current state-of-the-art deep learning-based methods, thanks to its efficient use of visual templates. Notably, an ensemble of PatchNet models trained on progressively larger training sets allows the model to adapt to a wide range of visual benchmarks, even when the training data is not specifically tailored to them. When compared to traditional computer vision methods, PatchNet's results, though obtained from a relatively small training set, significantly outperform them, showcasing the method's generalization capabilities. To facilitate the practical use of PatchNet, an efficient and scalable implementation is made available, allowing it to achieve real-time

We examine a one-dimensional, multi-species version of the TASEF model, where several species of particles move in both directions on a lattice, each having unique arrival and departure schedules at fixed time intervals. Particles following regular patterns are initially placed on the lattice, and we determine their final positions as they move over a specified number of time intervals, distributing themselves in the process. This distribution is shown to be a unique solution by a combination of arguments including a proof of asymptotic independence of different species of particles, and the existence of a stationary state under specific conditions. The research is based on prior studies of TASEF, KMS condition, and Kostilenko-Sheffield's work on the TASEF's oligopolistic equilibrium.

This study investigates how energy and data transmission coexist in dual-functional wireless systems. We develop a framework to optimize power allocation and data rate splitting for multiple users within these systems, given that each user has a unique pair of energy and data transfer requirements. We formulate a dual problem for this optimization and propose a iterative algorithm to solve it. Notably, this algorithm ensures that data rate splits for each user do not exceed their maximum possible values. Simulation results demonstrate that our algorithm achieves nearly optimal performance. Furthermore, we examine how system parameters influence the suboptimal data rate splits obtained from this algorithm, which reveals useful insights for system design.

Researchers have suggested an alternative general framework for the theoretical description of a particular type of Fermi mixture, which could be applied to both attractive and repulsive mixtures. In this study, we challenge the idea that this framework is universally applicable to repulsive Fermi mixtures by comparing its predictions to experimental results from a specific type of mixture. The framework assumes that the mixture's phases are determined by the parameters in a specific theoretical model, but we find that this assumption does not hold in our experimental results. Additionally, we observe that the rates of phase transition change can vary significantly depending on the parameters in the mixture, which contradicts a key prediction of the framework. These findings highlight the need for further development in the theoretical description of repulsive Fermi mixtures.

We present a simple electrical circuit model that mimics specific aspects of microwave optomechanics. Our proposed model consists of a parallel RLC circuit coupled to a resistive network including, for instance, an intracellular membrane with properties of series and parallel resistance. Mechanically, this biophysical membrane represents a seismically coupled boundary to a mechanical chamber, which is itself coupled to a driven microwave transmission line via a port with characteristics defined by its admittance. Our model utilizes a telegrapher matrix to analyze the time-dependent behavior of the system and we find that its time-dependent transmission spectrum displays phenomena analogous to typical optomechanical systems. Additionally, we are able to derive analytically the well-known Hopf bifurcation observed in time-independent optomechanical systems and we find that our model accurately reproduces the well-known Hopf bifurcation and associated phase transitions as a function of the mechanical driving force.

Witten's $Q$-box graph theory originates from two distinct sources - airship structure and matrix perturbation - which are connected to the focus on non-interacting fermions in specific geometric constraints. The $Q$-box graph is defined by an $N\times N$ matrix that represents the inverse of an $N\times N$ semi-definite perturbation matrix applied to an $M$-dimensional free fermion system or an $M$-fermion system confined within an $N$-dimensional space. The challenge lies in determining the determinant of such a matrix for given parameters $M$ and $N$, known as the $Q$-box determinant or $\Delta_M(N)$. This study establishes that this determinant has a general Airy polynomial form, denoted as $A_{M-N}(\xi)$. The proof involves breaking it down into two specific 1D fermion systems, each described by a specific Hamiltonian, and applying Calogero-Moshe-Gershgorin disc theorem to reduce them further. The resulting expression for $\Delta_M(N)$ is then connected to a symmetric eigenvalue problem of an $M$-fermion system, proving a key conjecture by Paquette et al. as a special case. The determinant $\Delta_M(N)$ is shown to exhibit a diverse, expansive pattern that encompasses numerous known determinants and extends beyond that.

Successful execution of the Complex Predictable Assembly Task (CPAT) requires robots to withstand disruptions of varying severity in the task environment. In preparation, we examined how robots respond to unexpected obstacles in assembling a simple box-like structure. Our study involved robots adhering to barriers, and investigating whether their reactions to small and large challenges could be anticipated. Upon analyzing robot performance in a standardized setup, we discovered that instead of expecting robots to persevere against smaller disturbances, the situation is more complicated - smaller obstacles sometimes prompt more substantial movements from the robots, contradicting initial expectations. Consequently, predicting how a robot will respond to a given disturbance becomes even more difficult than expected. Our study provides valuable insights for designing and modifying CPAT, enhancing robots' ability to assemble complex objects.

This article further explores and develops the concept of chiral aspects in 2dcft within the pAQFT framework, building upon a previously published study.  It specifically investigates how these aspects relate to a massless scalar field in globally hyperbolic 2-dimensional spacetimes.  The study identifies subalgebras that contain either chiral or anti-chiral observables, constructing these explicitly and showing they are embedded in the full theory's algebra.  It also establishes that the construction of these subalgebras is Cauchy surface-independent and yields a well-defined covariant theory on the space of null geodesics.

Smoke presence during laparoscopic surgery has been extensively examined in previous research, as its effects on hazy video images have made it a focus of many studies. Smoke reduction methods utilizing image processing techniques have been proposed to clarify the operating field, but few studies have investigated the feasibility of image enhancement to detect smoke presence. In this study, smoke detection using image processing techniques was compared on both smoke-added videos with and without smoke reduction methods. Smoke detection accuracy was assessed based on precision, recall, and F1 score metrics. Our findings show that smoke presence could be accurately predicted from hazy video images in both cases, but a notable observation is that smoke reduction methods do not necessarily improve the accuracy of smoke detection. Consequently, we conclude that smoke reduction methods are not a prerequisite for accurate smoke detection.

A Molmer-Sorensen gate's sensitivity to frequency changes can be the limiting factor in quantum computation using trapped ions, particularly when laser frequencies need to be matched precisely. To address this issue, we've developed a method to make MS gates more frequency-resistant by using a specific input sequence that distributes the initial atomic excitation equally across many degrees of freedom. By doing so, the average frequency mismatch is significantly reduced and nearly eliminated, resulting in a robust gate performance regardless of frequency errors. This breakthrough allows for the development of a more robust, frequency-independent quantum processor built with a small number of ions, leveraging the natural symmetry of its motion and input states.

To address the controversy surrounding temperature-dependent atomic pairs in BaTiO3 and other similar ferroelectric materials, we employed advanced electron backscatter diffraction and high-resolution microscopy. Our comprehensive analysis, combined with molecular dynamics simulations and extensive systematic searches, revealed the existence of a paraelectric phase at low temperatures. Our research provides a theoretical foundation for the paraelectric phase's microscopic appearance and suggests potential symptoms and Hallmarks to identify it experimentally.

Multivariate data that change over space or time can often be analyzed with a statistical model known as multivariate Gaussian distributions, with a specific type called graphical Gaussian distributions offering flexibility in modeling dependencies among data points. While this method can effectively capture relationships within individual data sets, it does not easily adapt to data that varies across multiple dimensions. A more comprehensive framework, called the functional Gaussian graphical framework, was developed to analyze such data by treating it as a special type of multivariate Gaussian distribution. In this research, we establish a direct relationship between graphical Gaussian distributions and the functional Gaussian graphical framework, allowing users to switch between these two frameworks by translating dependencies from one to the other. We further demonstrate how this relationship can be utilized in various applications, such as testing whether a process is stationary or non-stationary, and providing a more general approach to modeling dependent data by combining multiple processes.

In constructing a quantum circuit using repetitive units such as gates, the conventional approach involves combining identical components to form a single, lower-dimensional circuit. We investigate an alternative method of circuit assembly, which doesn't rely on grouping similar elements. Our first strategy generates random configurations of the circuit units. We also develop a deterministic procedure, inspired by a well-known random configuration, which produces a wide range of unique circuit components. We calculate the probability that two randomly assembled circuits from our deterministic method are equivalent to those from the traditional approach. We further extend our deterministic method to incorporate fractional symmetry to broaden its application and make it adaptable to various symmetry types. We calculate the probability that the assembled circuits, using our extended method, are equivalent to those from the conventional approach. We also evaluate the computational complexity of our deterministic methods.

A recent development in learning deep neural networks has revealed that under certain conditions, using a simple "ReLU" derivative function in a learning algorithm results in consistent, nearly error-free outcomes with arbitrarily large datasets. However, the exception to this rule involves neural networks with "threshold" or "sign" activation functions, requiring an additional assumption about the data in order to achieve similar results. The question arises as to whether these outcomes can occur without this additional data constraint. This research provides a mathematical justification for using a robust form of statistical analysis, leading to a surprising conclusion: even when the data is not follows a specific distribution, using a simple "sign" or "threshold" based learning algorithm can still produce consistent outcomes with large datasets. The size requirement for this consistency to occur involves a complex condition related to the capacity of the neural network, known as "information complexity," first described by David Pollard in the 1990s. A related concept, known as "stretch," is also explored in this research as it relates to neural networks and learning algorithms.

We investigate a bilayer semiconductor system with indirect gaps, characterized by
interlayer electron-hole pairs that condense into excitonic interlayers with strongly coupled
electrons and holes. Nonparabolic excitons form there due to interaction with the quantum fluid's
electrons which limits their diffusion. This polaron-like effect on excitons is the primary focus.
Moreover, we find that the trapping of excitons within the quantum fluid's strong interaction region
has a significant impact on the system's thermal equilibrium distribution.
Additionally, our analysis reveals that the bilayer excitonic system exhibits non-ergodic behavior,
characterized by a non-extensive entropy that increases with time.
Ultimately, our findings shed light on the common characteristics between bilayer excitonic conductors
and more well-known polaron-based systems, such as bilayer WSe2.

Self-adaptive systems that can adjust to variations in environment and respond effectively to unexpected changes in operation are crucial. The reliability of these systems heavily depends on accurate predictive models, which can be compromised by unanticipated events. This work focuses on securing the potential vulnerabilities of a part of an autonomous vehicle's adaptive system by developing an resilient radio-based localization and tracking process. A key challenge in this task is determining the occurrence of unexpected events and forecasting the changes they bring. A novel algorithm using a specific approach was developed to make reliable predictions, but it requires validation through thorough testing to confirm its effectiveness in real-world scenarios. Two types of testing were undertaken to assess the performance of this model on localized datasets: simulation testing with varied parameters and analysis of real-world data with adverse conditions. The outcome of these tests indicates that the proposed model can successfully predict and adapt to unexpected events and perform accurately in diverse scenarios.

Measurements of transverse polarisation components for $W$ and $Z$ bosons are reported.
Data from $pp$ collisions with a centre-of-mass energy of 13 TeV and 36.1 fb^-1 of integrated luminosity are used.
$W$ boson measurements in decay modes $W^{\pm} \rightarrow \mu^{\pm} \nu_{\mu}$ and $W^{\pm} \rightarrow e^{\pm} \nu_e$ are made.
$Z$ boson measurements in decay modes $Z \rightarrow \mu^{\pm} \mu^{\pm}$ and $Z \rightarrow e^{\pm} e^{\pm}$ are made.
Feynman gauge gives a fully parallel initial $W$ and $Z$ boson state which is confirmed.
$W$ and $Z$ boson properties are investigated in events with large transverse momentum.
No deviation from the standard model predictions is found.
An energy resolution of 7-8 GeV is achieved for $W$ and $Z$ bosons with high transverse momentum.
An analysis of cross-section and differential cross-section for $W$ and $Z$ boson production is made.
An interpretation of the findings based on the standard model and beyond the standard model is made and the results are presented.

A widespread misconception persists regarding the definition of gravity's source, 
attributing it solely to matter. A more accurate perspective is offered in this work, 
where any gravitational effect can be attributed to a tensor's appearance, specifically 
the Cotton tensor, and is further illustrated through a detailed derivation in four 
spacetime dimensions.

This research reveals a geometric duality for certain kinds of ordered structures known as orthocomplemented lattices, analogous to Mvalves duality for finite distributive lattices. Additionally, it introduces a geometric representation for coreflexive subsets of any finite distributive lattice, drawing comparisons with existing works such as Lal\'{e}char\'{e}'s geometric interpretation of finite distributive lattices and Benov\'{a}zdov\'{a}'s introduction of hypergroups as a dual form for finite distributive lattices.

We introduce a visualization tool, coq-psv, which generates interactive
visualizations from Coq proof scripts to facilitate students' learning the
Fourier-Merle proof. This can be achieved by running the tool on a proof script
in the Emacs algebraic geometry kernel. coq-psv aims to simplify the process
of comprehending the Fourier-Merle proof by visualizing key steps and
highlighting why certain lemmas are necessary. This is accomplished by
maintaining a record of relevant meta information as users navigate through
proofs. coq-psv then translates this data into interactive widgets to illustrate
the underlying concepts. For instance, one feature shows that certain lemmas
are only required if the proof branches diverge. coq-psv is now freely
available on GitHub.

We demonstrate that the fourth moment of holomorphic Hecke cusp forms is limited under the assumption of the Riemann Hypothesis for a specific degree 8 L-function. This is achieved by leveraging an argument initially put forth by Iwaniec and Sarnak. Our analysis also yields an asymptotic expression which suggests that the central value of the ratio of Hecke L-functions squared tends towards infinity as the level increases.

In interior point methods (IPMs), where we solve a problem that involves an equation with a positive Hessian and residuals, we often use the conjugate gradient method to solve the positive definite symmetric system. Researchers have found that the standard termination criterion for the conjugate gradient method does not work well with the interior point methods as it can lead to slow convergence or even wrong solutions. In this paper, we explore this issue and propose a new termination criterion that has been successful with interior point methods. The new criterion works by checking the direction in which the residual decreases most quickly, and has been found to provide substantial improvements in convergence time. In fact, with smaller problem sizes, the new criterion can lead to faster solution times than the conventional method. Furthermore, the interior point methods that use the new termination criterion demonstrate superior overall performance compared to those with the conventional method. Notably, the biggest speedup was observed with smaller problem sizes, indicating that the interior point methods can now be effectively used to solve even larger problems.

We have derived the $O(\alpha_s^3)$ series for the spin-dependent color-singlet transition matrix for quarks, and our findings are in line with the light-by-light diagram contribution to the polarized structure function $F_2^{\rm pol}(x)$. We also obtained the quark polarisation function $\tilde{G}_q^{(3)}(N^2)$ up to $O(\alpha_s^3)$. Our results facilitate a precise calculation of the spin-dependent flavor QCD corrections in deep-inelastic scattering at $O(\alpha_s^3)$.

The incorporation of artificial intelligence into various sectors has brought about significant benefits, yet it has also led to unforeseen negative outcomes on a global scale, underscoring the need for AI research to align with real-world objectives. A major obstacle to progress is the scarcity of accessible data on AI incidents, hindering efforts to identify common patterns and prevent similar incidents from recurring. In response, we establish the AI Incident Repository (AIR), a comprehensive database of notable AI incidents, along with suggested classification models and search queries to retrieve related research, with the ultimate goal of advising AI practitioners on how to avoid replicating these incidents in their own research and practice.

A new adaptive renormalization group technique has been created, allowing it to effectively navigate complex systems by continuously transforming them until they become trivial in character. By employing a learned gradient descent algorithm, informed by minimal assumptions, it can identify and eliminate non-critical features in a system, providing a simplified yet accurate representation. This simplified representation retains only the essential information necessary to describe the system's essential behavior. This technique can be applied broadly, covering both statistical systems and quantum field theories, and is independent of any underlying action or Hamiltonian. It can also be used to identify critical dimensions in renormalization group flow.
