Furthermore, it can be applied to strongly coupled systems, such as those with relevant operators with high dimensionality. It has semi-algorithmic characteristics, with some parts being adaptable based on underlying principles. It can be viewed as a non-standard implementation of the renormalization group, which can still provide semi-quantitative and qualitative insights. It has potential uses in fundamental theory, but may raise concerns about its ability to be precise due to its adaptive nature.

Business processes that incorporate human decision-making activities, such as assessing claims and resolving disputes, are scrutinized by regulatory bodies. To address concerns about unfair processing, these authorities demand that businesses develop and adapt formal models describing the evolution of business processes over time. Unfortunately, existing methodologies limiting human influence often lead to overly restrictive model adaptations, hindering a vital aspect of human decision-making: the management of disputes. To address this, we propose a new monitoring method capable of detecting violations related to dispute resolution, taking into account the dual processes of business operations that incorporate human decision-making activities. To adapt the model, we introduce a novel technique, Dual-Automaton, which allows for the simultaneous construction of two interconnected infinite paths representing the dual processes. To identify discrepancies between these paths and the actual dispute management steps recorded with the help of tools like process mining, we outline a monitoring strategy, Dispute Monitoring, capable of detecting discrepancies and generating a structured format for reporting violations that could be used to improve dispute resolution steps. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we present a real-world use case involving the Italian Public Administration, showing how the proposed method enables the detection and resolution of issues related to the negotiation of disputes.

Quipper, a domain-specific language, is designed to efficiently compile circuit-based quantum programs. Its prototype, Quipper-M, is an expressive extension of the standard language, featuring higher-order functions and mutable reference cells. The original paper on Quipper-M lacks a formal semantics, relying solely on observational equivalence to evaluate the program's behavior. This omission hampers theoretical analysis and practical verification tools. To address this gap, we propose a structured interpretation of Quipper-M that incorporates continuations, recursive operators, and recursive reference cells. Our proposed semantics is justified by a by-product reduction theorem, demonstrating that the underlying abstract machine's external behavior matches the predicted results from the structured semantics.

We examine the behavior of rare events in random matrices, specifically their tendency to appear on the boundary of significant occurrences. We show that these events exhibit distinct scaling patterns in relation to their frequency, leading to separate regimes of typical and atypical behavior. We apply our findings to the study of larval dynamics through a stochastic matrix representing the transition probabilities of a Markov process. We discover that the distribution of extreme events can be described by a statistical physics framework, resulting in a Gaussian distribution with parameters that vary depending on the system's dimensions. We further analyze the distribution of these extreme events and find that its center or average value follows a different statistical physics framework, leading to a different dimensional dependence. Our study provides a comprehensive description of typical and atypical behavior in random matrices and a precise classification of extreme events.

We suggest creating pairs of bosons in a cavity using SCMO dipoles linked to an optical cavity. These dipoles have two energy levels that can interact with photons in the cavity, allowing for the production of bosonic pairs through a continuous optical pulse. We investigate the pair generation and squeezing of the optical field in the cavity using a quantum optical pulse characterised by a amplitude-squeezed Gaussian laser beam. Our findings indicate that when the cavity is in a specific, optimised state, nearly complete pair generation occurs along with substantial squeezing of the optical field. We define and apply an efficiency metric to evaluate pair generation, and demonstrate that a high level of squeezing in the optical field is associated with a high efficiency of bosonic pair generation.

Assembling complete and error-free genomes from a large number of long, artificial DNA sequences, referred to as contigs, is an extremely computationally intensive task. Due to the rapidly increasing DNA sequence data, researchers face an increasingly daunting computational challenge. In order to alleviate this burden, we have developed a new, parallel algorithm for contig creation using compact, shared memory approaches. By utilizing a novel strategy of randomly distributing overlapping DNA sequences to compute edit distances, we have designed an efficient, shared-memory approach for determining the most suitable sequence combinations. This innovative method, being both simple and efficient, achieves outstanding performance on massive datasets, surpassing by a significant margin the performance of existing, node-memory parallel schemes. Furthermore, we have also successfully implemented and tested this approach in a distributed-memory system utilizing high-speed data communication, resulting in consistent results comparable to that of the shared-memory approach.

A thorough analysis is conducted on the global properties of a newly proposed equation, $dN/dt=\psi(N)$, with $\psi(N)$ following a delayed logistic pattern, specifically, $\lambda N/(1+N^k)\cdot\exp(-\beta N)$. 

This investigation emerges from a theoretical model exploring the evolution of species without competition for resources, instead focusing on the positive interactions between organisms and their environment. 

The study shows that the equation has an endlessly expanding solution for large $N>0$, and using phase plane methods and singular perturbation techniques, we identify asymptotically stable solutions. 

Our work includes a summary of well-known biological models in ecology and their connections to the delayed logistic equation, in addition to examining the equation's solutions approaching zero.

Heffron and Alldredge introduced the concept of statistical depth from temporal series data in 2010. In this work, we develop a new depth measure applicable to data represented by point procedures. To achieve this, we propose an alternative representation of the data using the inverse of a specific function, followed by a Gaussian random variable. This approach can be seen as a extension of the Cauchy depth formula, as previously formulated by Crouzeilles and Garel. A depth measure based on the new representation is defined by utilizing the distribution's quantiles under the generalized Cauchy distribution. This formulation results in a new depth measure, which we prove to possess the desired properties, including invariance to location and scale parameters. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the new depth measure in analyzing data from a solar navigation system.

A particular setup consisting of a quantum capacitor made from a superconductor and a quantum point contact has been created and studied with detailed analysis using an experimental technique known as scanning gate spectroscopy, alongside comprehensive theoretical modeling. In an ideal scenario, this device exhibits distinctive spectral patterns within its density of states. However, when the superconductor's temperature is below its critical point but not in a state of perfect conductivity, these patterns disappear due to interference caused by quasi-particles' interactions. Despite the absence of these ideal features, our study demonstrates the significant impact of quasi-particle interactions on spectral patterns and validates a long-standing theoretical model describing these interactions in a specific context. Additionally, our research highlights the importance of carefully controlling device characteristics to accurately reproduce and analyze experimental results.

Study was conducted on isotopes of germanium with an emphasis on those near $N$ = 40, as these are known to be part of the nuclear shell. Using the LUNDER module within the GOGAM2D+GOGAM electron scattering analysis, atomic moments were calculated for 35Ge to 45Ge. These moments revealed a shell closure at $N$ = 40, characterized by a significantly reduced nuclear deformation. Notably, 39Ge showed a non-spherical nuclear structure, whereas 41Ge had a nearly spherical shape. These findings were also supported by a collective model of the nuclear interaction, confirming the occurrence of a shell closure at $N$ = 40.

Researchers have introduced an innovative method for making precise mass measurements using the ISOLDE B\rho facility. This method leverages the concept of isochronous mass spectrometry, combining the strengths of the Double-Linear-Ion-Trap mass spectrometer to achieve high-precision mass measurements with minimal uncertainty. This technique enabled the measurement of the mass-to-charge ratio of the exotic nucleus $^{22}$Na with an uncertainty of $4.1\times 10^{-8}$, serving as a reference for calculating the atomic mass of nafrate chelate nafrate na$_2$F$_3$ with an uncertainty of $7.7\times 10^{-10}$. Furthermore, this study discusses the potential of this method for making precise mass measurements of transient nuclei.

The SQuID project aims to create an open-source library for quantum lattice field theory simulations to support research in various domains, such as quantum physics, quantum gravity, and black hole theory. The SQuID library focuses on developing reusable software components, known as units, that can easily be combined and executed on different quantum processors. This approach facilitates standardized calculations, and the library aims to provide a comprehensive framework for quantum lattice field theory simulations. The SQuID library is designed to support users with little to no quantum experience, and we document our development process to provide insight into the challenges we face. This presentation focuses on the details of our unit design and the benefits of a standardized calculation workflow within the library.

To enhance text classification, it's crucial to locate and isolate organized text inputs, but this identification process is highly complex due to the numerous possible formats of organized data. Research has shown that Enhanced LM can significantly improve text generation by promoting the usage of favorable regular expression patterns, resulting in more efficient identification of complex, structured text inputs. By applying this technology to the field of text classification, we aim to develop a more robust method for identifying and isolating complex, organized text inputs, which will in turn enhance the performance of classification models.

The LHCb experiment has demonstrated the capacity to identify the creation of top quarks in high-energy proton-lead collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. Utilizing data from a 7 TeV proton-proton collision run, with an integrated luminosity of approximately 3 inverse picobarns, and further supplemented with lead-proton collisions at 8.16 TeV, with a 0.1 inverse nanobarns integrated luminosity. The experiment successfully detected the signatures of top quark production in two distinct events, specifically the electron-positron and muon-muon pairs resulting from the decay of intermediate bosons. The observed creations of these signatures exhibit a statistical significance of up to 3.1 standard deviations above the predicted levels of background noise. The measured properties of these events align with the theoretical predictions of mass 173 GeV for the top quark. The experiment has established a lower bound on the cross-sectional ratio of top quark creation in proton-lead collisions to proton-proton collisions at the same energy level, with a 95% confidence interval. Additionally, the experiment has set a new boundary on the fraction of inclusive dispersed jet productions in proton-proton collisions at 7 TeV, with a 95% confidence interval.

We address the challenge of translating any text into valid SQL queries across various domains. Existing methods, though successful in limited datasets like SQL-NLP and SQL-Fashion, struggle with vast and complex real-world datasets such as Spider. To bridge the gap, we introduce two novel parsing tasks: "What's the focus?" and "What's the price of?", both extracting specific information from a given sentence. We demonstrate that a parser trained on datasets like Spider, enhanced by these tasks, can effectively translate any text into valid SQL queries across any given dataset. We've made our code and data available for public use.

The LoTSS, a comprehensive survey of the northern sky using the LoFAR radio observatory, has released its initial data set comprising 99 low-frequency radio sources with high spectral resolution. These sources were detected over 353 square degrees of sky and exhibit spectral ranges of up to 228 kHz. By cross-referencing LoTSS with WISDOM kinematic data and having accessed early LOFAR data via the pilot LoTSS, we studied the characteristics of galaxies' energy spectra and radio source biasing. Our analysis indicates that the width of galaxies' energy spectra correlates positively with their stellar masses and morphological types, as well as logarithmetic mass of galaxies. Furthermore, we discovered two distinct classes of source biasing, comprising sources with stable spectra and significant redshifts, and sources with degraded spectra and lower redshifts. Our findings from LoTSS confirm and extend previous observations based on smaller datasets, suggesting that the relationship between radio emission and galactic mass is intricate and influenced by multiple factors.

The High-Dimensional Rank Lasso (HDL) model utilizes the penalized maximum-likelihood estimation method to solve the problem of recovering a low-rank matrix from a large number of noisy measurements. The Rank Lasso model was first introduced as an effective approach to meeting this goal, but its high computational complexity made it impractical for large datasets. As a result, there is a pressing need for an efficient algorithm to solve the Rank Lasso problem, especially for datasets exceeding 10,000 variables. In this research, we present an adaptive sifting algorithm, referred to as 2AS-1sc, which builds on an earlier adaptive sifting method and significantly reduces the computational complexity associated with finding the Hessian matrix. The 2AS-1sc method offers a straightforward extension to work with block-structured problems, yielding an efficient block sifting algorithm, or BS method, when combined with an optimal binary partition strategy. The 2AS-1sc method is then refined to include a sampling technique, creating a new algorithm, or S-2AS-1sc, which utilizes sampled information to lower the computational complexity of its inner loop. The 2AS-1sc method is compared to other established methods, including ADMM, block-structured algorithms such as Block-Procrustes, and sampling-based algorithms such as Conjugate Gradient, through extensive numerical testing with artificially generated data. These experiments consistently demonstrate the superior performance of the S-2AS-1sc method

We examine the rate of entropy production in small systems undergoing driven processes. This is analyzed by considering a thermal bath with a complex eigenvalue spectrum, which results in an uneven distribution of eigenvalues. These characteristics are examined in detail, including how a system's rate of entropy production is influenced by its initial state, thermal contact, and external influence. This analysis sheds light on the condition required for a system to maintain a low rate of entropy production and verifies this through a study of a driven spin-1/2 system. This research demonstrates that a particular method of minimizing entropy production can be effectively applied even under moderate driving forces and rapid external influences.

Artificial intelligence has earned its place as a key environmental solution due to its capabilities for high-precision environmental monitoring, efficient management of resources, and accurate prediction of potential threats. However, the solutions AI implements to address environmental challenges frequently overlook one vital aspect - the environmental impact of the technologies themselves. For instance, developing and utilizing AI necessitates significant amounts of energy and computational resources, which in turn necessitate the usage of non-renewable materials and infrastructure. This research aims to identify, evaluate, and mitigate these hidden effects, classifying them into direct and indirect influences, and proposing actionable strategies for designers and policymakers to address these significant but understated challenges.

Prescriptive process monitoring, a subcategory of business process management, involves detecting issues early in a process execution to prevent or mitigate negative consequences. A prescriptive system can provide a risk score for each process instance as it unfolds, flag problem areas and suggest corrective actions to avoid deviations. A prescriptive process system is ideal for high-stakes business processes where even minor setbacks can have substantial financial impacts. Due to its potential benefits, research has been conducting a systematic review of prescriptive process monitoring to assess its state-of-the-art. The analysis reveals a dearth of relevant business processes and empirical studies. It appears that prescriptive process monitoring has not been effectively implemented in real-world settings. The review's findings indicate a need for more practical approaches to prescriptive process monitoring and suggest broadening its definition to include early descriptive processes. Future prescriptive process A/R research should be grounded in practical considerations and grounded in ongoing BPM research.

We introduce an innovative approach to mistake detection and correction in numerical simulations of fluid flow heat transfer, employing the generalized Boussinesq model. This model seeks to minimize discrepancies between measured temperatures and predicted temperatures in heat transfer applications. By formulating a goal-oriented adaptive finite element method, we optimize the finite element solution, aligning it with measured temperature data, thus reducing errors. This strategy is versatile and can be applied with various goal-oriented adaptation techniques. We illustrate the efficacy of this method in heated fluid flow systems using two distinct sets of experimental data.

Research into combinatorial optimization problems with specific limitations and restrictions on their input has shown that many stacking-type problems, including key ones like Dominating Set and Oriented Dominating Set, can be solved efficiently when limited to restricted input scenarios. We investigate how to apply this knowledge to obtain more powerful reduction techniques, specifically kernelizations, for these problems. Our study reveals that, besides Oriented Dominating Set, no other problem has a polynomial-time kernelization. However, it is unclear whether kernelizations exist or not for all problems with at most two vertices. To better understand this uncertainty, we also examine the limitations of reduction techniques involving graph embeddings. Our findings show that no problem involving a single vertex can have a kernelization involving an embedding. This result is proven by demonstrating the incompatibility of two reduction techniques – polynomial kernelizations and embeddings with the NODWHS problem combined. Our reductions, including a new one for Oriented Dominating Set, play a crucial role in establishing this incompatibility. Additionally, we present an initial experiment to obtain a kernel for Dominating Set in planar graphs with layered structure. The obtained kernel is shown to be efficiently tractable in terms of time complexity. This finding inspires the proposal of a new concept, called layering width, which might be valuable for further examination.

In asynchronous, sequential, and confidential interactions with untrusted parties, networked systems rely on preferential exchanges of information to function. This information exchange is constrained by participants' differing opinions on the systems' internal workings. This study introduces a model to analyze these exchanges and their effects on the systems' operation. The model separates these exchanges into two types: primary information shared at the start, and ongoing exchanges based on each party's relative confidence level. The study examines how these exchanges impact the systems, identifying scenarios where the systems' internal processes reach a stable equilibrium and others where they fluctuate indefinitely. When in equilibrium, the systems' behavior may provide limited assurance of their correct operation, even though participants hold varying opinions. Conversely, ongoing exchanges can lead to shifting perceptions of the systems' reliability. Through this model, the study provides framework and methodology guidelines for understanding these information exchanges and their impact on dependent systems in high-level abstractions, including human-made and living biological systems.

A level fuzzy set is a fundamental concept that can be applied to different domains, leading to two types of fuzzy sets, referred to as crisp and fuzzy sets. Utilizing level sets of a fuzzy set, researchers have studied their inner properties, specifically the interior of an asymptotically level fuzzy set. Building on this, a complete characterization of the interior of fuzzy sets is presented, along with an investigation of their minimal and maximal values. Additionally, the study examines the relationship between cut sets and nested fuzzy sets.

A significant issue in studying transcription has been the lack of data on the temporal relationships between nearby genes' activation states, but recent advancements in single-molecule real-time monitoring of transcription have made possible the collection of transcription data for every gene across the entire S. cerevisiae genome at a high resolution in multiple conditions. Comparing this with existing genome-wide chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing data on various transcription factors, we observed considerable disparities in the ordering of nearby genes within the same operon or adjacent on a chromosome. These ordering differences led to two possible interpretations: first, there may be a time lag between when a transcription factor starts controlling a gene and when it controls a neighboring one, or second, there may be a significant distance-dependent interaction between transcription factors and the enzymes converting them into active forms. To address these possibilities, we developed a model-based approach for analyzing the relative temporal relationships between groups of transcription factors targeting distinct sets of genes, and our results from extensive simulations using the generated transcription data confirmed the presence of significant lags between when genes start to be transcribed and when they finish transcribing. Notably, the lags we identified were consistent across multiple observation times, as well as across various observation intervals. Moreover, we demonstrated that these lags could be predicted from the available chromatin IP data before the experiments were even conducted. Our study provides a framework for estimating the temporal relationships between transcription events using single-molecule real-time monitoring data, and reveals a previously unobserved

Recent findings on 64Ni's energy levels by  Zn91-driven 58.5 MeV beams have uncovered new data that shed light on the nucleus's structure, particularly regarding its low-lying systems. These discoveries reveal two- and three-body bound states comprising a core and one or two protons. Notably, a previously unknown 0+ state at 3835.7 keV was discovered, alongside existing 0+, 2, and 0 states. By incorporating the monopole tensor interaction into the shell model, the researchers have been able to accurately predict the 64Ni system's structure, including the previously unknown 0+ state's placement. This prediction validates the monopole tensor interaction's significance in understanding coupled systems.

Chiral SU(N) gauge theories in 2d/3d/4d spacetimes exhibit unique characteristics due to the absence of fermion redundancies and are thereby defined solely by an orientable 2-manifold that wraps around the compact manifold of the theory. We explore and outline recent breakthroughs in establishing dualities for SU(N) theories from both supersymmetric and non-supersymmetric models. Specifically, we discuss how Seiberg theory generalizations, monopole and quark operators, and relevant chiral operators are integral components of these dualities. Furthermore, we examine the specific examples of dualities for SU(2) and SU(3) theories.

A linear complementary set of group codes consists of pairs of group codes with identical parameters that have minimal pairwise intersection. We establish a criterion for the existence of linear complementary sets of group codes of order m and rank n, with the selector set being an abelian group of order d, particularly when the codes have a square order and the selector set has a square order as well. This criterion leads to the finding of linear complementary sets of certain group codes of orders 16, 25, 29, and 65. Additionally, we outline a general method for constructing linear sets of group codes.

We introduce a new, compact representation of a function that significantly reduces computational and storage requirements, allowing for the depiction of a function within a structure's variable sequence. This new representation, called a 'brief function depiction' (BFD), uses variable ranges and specific network structure properties to minimize the description of a function. We utilize this representation to develop more efficient algorithms for exact memory and computation constraints in MPE tasks and show a direct relationship between BFD and the maximum joint mutual information within a network. Additionally, we demonstrate that BFD facilitates faster optimization within specific graphical models, particularly in those with chain or circular structures.

Individuals with mobility issues or limited visibility can face significant challenges in finding an item that is out of sight. However, advances in audio and visual technology enable the development of innovative solutions that can effectively support both groups by accurately localizing hard-to-reach items and informing them of their locations. Building on the success of existing research, we introduce a novel method that utilizes asynchronous audio-visual data fusion to improve the accuracy of visual cameras in pinpointing target locations more precisely. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed approach surpasses current state-of-the-art solutions in a practical, real-world scenario involving the localization of prone items.

One of the main factors that contributes to the slowing down of tumbling particles suspended in a fluid is the enhancement of their rotational resistance due to interactions with neighboring particles. Understanding how particle arrangements affect this resistance is crucial for making predictions about particle movement and behavior. In this study, we examined the global patterns of rotation resistance in densely packed suspensions of elongated particles and discovered specific particle arrangements that cause a significant increase in resistance. Additionally, we found that these critical arrangements occur less frequently as particle densities increase, resulting in varying levels of resistance at different particle densities. We found that these variations in resistance can significantly impact the movement of particles in certain situations.

During periods of high electricity consumption, such as hot summer days, a power shortage occurs. In order to prevent and mitigate power shortages, it is essential to understand how electricity consumption behaves under these conditions. However, since data on these situations is often limited, this research utilizes simulated data based on real usage patterns from the 2003 US New England power crisis. An hourly analysis of this simulated data indicates that electricity consumption is governed by a beta distribution, specifically a form known as the Pearson Type I distribution, which is also applicable to longer-term periods of peak consumption. As a result, this research provides a logical explanation for this phenomenon and provides a practical statistical model for forecasting electricity consumption during power crisis phases.

A significant body of research under the term "filter bubbles" hypothesize that personalization can isolate users from diverse viewpoints.  We take a closer look at this concept through the lens of human cognition and find that personalization may be more subtle than commonly believed.  Our study involves analyzing news articles from Google News, examining their relationships with other articles on the platform using citations as relationships' direction indicators.  Our findings show that users may miss a substantial amount of pertinent information due to Google's search customization - approximately 24% on average, with some searches underrepresented by as much as 57% of relevant information.  To mitigate this, we suggest combining algorithms that take both cognitive biases and users' inherent limitations into account, going beyond the present state of the art in customization systems.

Graph representation learning plays a crucial role in program visualization when translating flow diagrams into source code, but our novel GRCNN approach simplifies this process by automatically learning graph features. In contrast to previous methods, which defined graph structures before feeding them to convolutional neural networks, our GRCNN method generates the graph structure itself. Our findings demonstrate that GRCNN outperforms other state-of-the-art approaches on a wide range of benchmarks in graph-based code generation.

Climate research is becoming increasingly data-driven due to significant advancements in climate modelling and observational methods. The application of dynamical systems in climate analysis has expanded exponentially in recent decades. This growth in knowledge necessitates a systematic review of the various methods for simplifying dynamical models, which are essential for further investigation. This work aims to provide an in-depth overview of these methods, their applications, and potential avenues for further exploration, focusing on differential equations that are easily understandable.

The groundbreaking discovery of gravitational waves emanating from a binary neutron star merger in August 2017 paved the way for a new era in multimessenger astronomy. Kilonovae, produced by the expelled material from neutron star collisions, present an attractive opportunity for optical and near-infrared follow-up observations following the detection of gravitational waves. The observation of the kilonova from the GW170817 merger using multiple astronomical telescopes helped to reveal the behavior of the merger's ejecta as it interacted with the intense light emitted in the aftermath. Recent studies have led to a long-awaited calculation of the critical opacity values necessary for a thorough understanding of the kilonova light curves. Nonetheless, a pressing need remains for further computations concerning the less understood opacities within the merger ejecta. Consequently, a recent study has computed the essential data required for the systematic evaluation of opacity levels in the merger ejecta, focusing particularly on the Os isoelectronic sequence. This important research involved the computation of crucial energy levels and relative opacities for Os, Pt, Au, Hg, and Tl ions with low positive charges. This significant study, which we detail in this work, computes the essential data required for the systematic evaluation of opacity levels in the merger ejecta, focusing particularly on the Au isoelectronic sequence. A critical phase in creating computerized models of the GI tract is segmenting its various components. The goal of this process is to outline and differentiate the distinct structures within the abdominal cavity's CT images to facilitate accurate reconstruction of the gastrointestinal system. In this study, a cutting-edge U-Net-based model was developed to improve the segmentation of the GI tract's various structures through the incorporation of dilated convolutional layers and residual learning techniques. The proposed method significantly enhances the accuracy of manual segmentation outcomes, achieving a notable mean DICE score of 0.85 for the upper GI tract and 0.87 for the lower GI tract. The obtained results demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed technique when compared to the standard U-Net model.

Compositional data are a type of data where the sum of the components is constant, often consisting of percentages or fractions. They are found in fields like biology, chemistry, genetics, epidemiology and market research. Common coefficients used to represent these data include raw coefficients, log ratios and isometric log-ratio coefficients. Our focus lies on the practical application of these coefficients in the examination, visualization and interpretation of compositional data. We also introduce an easy-to-use R function that calculates and evaluates the effectiveness of prediction models based on the sum of the squared errors.

Previous research suggested that sub-Saturn mass exoplanets tend to occupy a 'desert region' characterized by longer orbital periods than expected for their masses. However, a statistical analysis of 97 Saturn-mass and smaller planets detected by CORALIE/HARPS with known masses and orbital periods did not support this 'desert region' hypothesis. In fact, the data showed a significant number of planets with orbital periods significantly shorter than predicted by theoretical models. This discrepancy persists across various planetary mass ranges and is consistent even when accounting for planetary evolution and systematic errors. While the reasons behind this discrepancy are unclear, it may be attributed to biases in planetary detection or a lack of fully developed planetary cores required for gas retention and subsequent planetary growth. Further research is needed to address these potential issues and reconcile theory with observation.

To address the issue of Attention Overfitting, we introduce a novel regulation technique called Mutual Knowledge Enhancement (MKE) which can be applied universally to various attention networks. MKE works by splitting the data into random subsets and utilizing one subset for primary training while using the other subset to assess the attention network's performance. During the assessment process, the model adjusts its attention weights dynamically in an iterative manner, incorporating knowledge from the primary training data. Our method is adaptable to both on-demand and batch training processes, demonstrating superior performance when compared to existing techniques in multiple image classification and text classification datasets.

To explore the possibility of dark matter composed of two fermions under a specific type of interaction, we investigate the behavior of a compressed fermionic system in two-dimensional space, including the occurrence of a Fermi arc. In the presence of a Yukawa interaction, we derive its gap equation, evaluate the impact of compression on the interaction, and discover that the Yukawa interaction can be represented as a specific type of compression-dependent force. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a compressed dark matter composition of two fermions with distinct masses is feasible, resulting in distinct dark matter particles with varying masses, and illustrating how the Yukawa interaction can be seen as a result of these fermions interacting with each other.

Neural networks learn more efficiently when some connections are disabled, despite having more parameters, and we've developed a simple method to achieve this using recurrent neurons. A single layer of neurons can solve a wide range of tasks, including modeling complex data and making predictions based on multiple inputs, and because these networks are relatively small, they can be trained quickly. We've shown that these networks can outperform larger ones in tasks such as recognizing patterns of different lengths, following a ball bounce, and predicting the movement of a hand, and our results suggest that using these networks could be a more effective way to tackle complex problems in neuroscience.

We establish a comprehensive method to classify nilpotent algebras based on their generators and relations, similar to classification systems for specific types of algebras, such as Lie or Jordan-Lie. The structure of such algebras is described through a correspondence in a geometric form. Furthermore, this work serves as a unifying thread, linking existing classification systems for specific types of algebras and providing insights into the properties of these algebras.

It is argued in this paper that black holes (including those in jets) should not form at redshifts above a certain threshold because matter at such high redshifts would prevent it from doing so. This conclusion is based on a study of how a black hole grows through the accretion of nearby intergalactic cloud material. It is found that at high redshifts, a massive black hole would not be able to form because it would not be able to grow quickly enough to overcome the obstacles in its path. In addition, it is found that even smaller black holes would be unable to form at such high redshifts because they would not have enough material to draw from in order to grow. In order to test these findings, a computer simulation was used to model a one-dimensional universe that is similar to our own, and it is found that a massive black hole would not be able to form until a certain point in time in the early history of the universe. A massive black hole would not be able to form until it reaches a certain amount of mass, at which point it would be able to overcome the obstacles in its path and continue growing. It is found that a massive black hole would not be able to exist for a significant period of time in the early history of the universe because it would not have enough material to draw from in order to grow. Researchers face a challenge in finding appropriate Lagrangians for general relativity, as the theory lacks a well-defined global action. We suggest two global actions for gravity in four dimensions, one of which utilizes a gauge-invariant approach and incorporates holonomies into the Lagrangian. We also explore the non-relativistic version of these Lagrangians, which corresponds to deformed Galilean gravity. We demonstrate that the relativistic and non-relativiable actions exhibit similar structures. Furthermore, we discuss how our gauge-invariant approach might be applied to modified gravity theories.

The primary goal of our research is to demonstrate the efficacy of three-dimensional Shortlist, a powerful image feature descriptor, in nonlinear MRI-based brain mapping, especially in cases where structural changes due to disorders such as multiple system atrophy, ataxin-3 expansion, and normal aging have led to significant alterations in brain anatomy. In a more general context, 3D Shortlist stands out for its superior performance in large-scale point-set registration, a task that also interests the computer vision community. One key characteristic of 3D Shortlist is its ability to efficiently handle extremely large point sets, which makes it an ideal candidate for applications involving partial or whole-brain derivatives. Another notable feature of 3D Shortlist is its robustness on volume data with varying resolutions, which is essential for accurately aligning brain maps. In addition, model-free registration using 3D Shortlist yields results that are invariant to image intensity variations, making it more suitable than other methods based on volume normalization. In our experiments, 3D Shortlist achieved state-of-the-art performance on the BRATS brain tumor dataset and demonstrated model-free convergence on diverse neurological and neurodegenerative diseases, including MSA, ataxin-3, and aging-related changes.

We conducted a comprehensive examination of the unique double-star system SDSS J082239.54+304857.19, known for its extremely short orbital period of 832 seconds. By utilizing the ZTF telescope, we captured detailed light curves of this system, revealing a more complex pattern than initially anticipated. Instead of a straightforward 832-second cycle, we detected multiple distinct phases, each lasting around 110 seconds. Furthermore, we identified a 40.5-minute cycle, likely a result of a secondary, longer orbital period overlap with our line-of-sight. By closely analyzing these findings, we inferred that the deeper 900-second valley of the system corresponds to a significant change in the system's behavior, and the presence of a longer orbital period companion is confirmed. By predicting the timings of these deeper minima, we created a detailed light curve pattern, and our observations matched this predicted pattern, providing further confirmation of the system's structure and properties.

It is well established that global aggregation in large collections of agents can be modeled using a simple, universal method outlined in the Tononi approach. This method is both intuitive and successful, yet it has a significant drawback - it completely fails to provide any clear agency to the individual agents within these collections. Drawing from ideas in information theory and dynamics, we propose an agency-based method for global aggregation that is rooted in the concept of transport. This new method is known as the Information Distance method and it shares a significant connection with the Fechner law, a well-known century-old empirical finding. When applied to basic decision-making tasks, it reveals a surprising connection with the concept of cover and the continuous lifestream model, demonstrating its strong agency grounding capabilities. Most notably, the Information Distance method demonstrates two key agency attributes - completeness and decidability. Furthermore, we develop a general procedure for deriving agency-based methods of global aggregation, agency-invariant methods that rely on the fundamental principles of transport. One such method is the angular information method. These agency-invariant methods possess a range of desirable properties including their ability to predict human behavior, as observed through crowd simulation studies, and their connection with the concept of mutual information. Finally, we investigate the relationship between agency-based methods and their inverse counterparts, revealing that the latter fail to capture key properties of agency, including the notion of actions and their consequences.

The primary objective of this research is to examine the host galaxies of AGNs classified in different types. By utilizing a large, comprehensive dataset consisting of more than 600,000 galaxies including over 120,000 which exhibit AGN activity, this study categorizes galaxies into various AGN types and compares their characteristics in terms of location, orientation, and physical properties. Notably, it has been discovered that the distribution of AGN types differs significantly depending on location, with higher prevalence of HII and LINERs in close proximity to the plane of the galaxy and a significant accumulation of composite and LLAGN around the edges. Moreover, it has been found that the prevailing host galaxy type and its magnetic field structure vary substantially depending on the AGN subtype, with star-forming galaxies predominantly harboring HII and LINERs, while spiral and elliptical galaxies are more likely to harbor composite and LLAGN, respectively. Additionally, the study provides the first large-scale analysis of the relationship between AGN activity and the large-scale structure of the galaxy, revealing that the prevailing orientation of the radio signal is not necessarily an indication of the dominant spiral arm, but rather it is significantly influenced by the local environment and the magnetic field of the galaxy.

This research paper presents a novel finding - a flat equatorial plane in a 4-dimensional Euclidean space that features a localized 1-type Gaussian map. Additionally, we have derived the distinct mean curvatures of this plane.

Deep neural network training for semantic segmentation requires extensive labelling efforts, making pre-training techniques with minimal input necessary to improve performance. Recent studies have demonstrated that depth estimation from single images can be accomplished with relatively simple models and little data, making it a feasible base for semantic segmentation tasks. Nonetheless, these models may not always reach top-notch accuracy in estimating depth. Consequently, we investigate whether depth assessment is a suitable pre-training method for semantic segmentation and consider the impact of the task's difficulty. Our study reveals that, contrary to expectations, depth estimation does not always facilitate semantic segmentation after adjustments for varying task complexities. In fact, classification, a fundamentally distinct task, often yields better results in our experiments. The reasons behind this outcome are explored in more detail.

We introduce TCube, a novel neural time-series storytelling approach that generates engaging, domain-agnostic stories for any input time-series data. Unlike previous methods, which often require predefined narrative structures, TCube can create various stories on its own. Our research includes an analysis of the difference between domain-specific and neutral storytelling and demonstrates that neutral stories better capture the overall data progression using multi-grained attention mechanisms. TCube is trained using a diverse set of texts and can generate stories compatible with the input data dynamics. Our experiments show that TCube significantly outperforms existing methods in creating neutral stories with relevant details, and we evaluate its performance both humanly and automatically. Our research aims to expand the neural storytelling framework to produce neutral stories that can serve as a starting point for further narrative enhancements. Our code is available on GitHub.

The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has made significant contributions in the fields of beauty-meson research, including investigations of rare and CP-violating decays. This study aims to provide an overview of the most advanced findings achieved by the ATLAS collaboration in this area of study.

On a Cayley tree, novel periodic and anti-periodic Ising model distributions have been discovered on large lattices for any desired period. These novel distributions defy the standard symmetry and inversion symmetry found in earlier studies. Furthermore, we've demonstrated that our novel distributions converge to unique invariant measures under certain scaling parameters.

In the study of hyperbolic partial differential equations, a new class of coefficients is defined where the distance between points and the distance between the points at which the initial conditions are specified each grow at a rate not much faster than logarithm of the distance. It is demonstrated that in this scenario, solutions to such equations can always be found and are well-defined for all times, provided the data they start with is suitable. Additionally, it is shown that solutions remain nearly unchanged regardless of small changes in the data they start with, and this holds true for all times. Notably, previous research has suggested that solutions may not always be well-defined for all times in this scenario, even with suitable data, and may not be robust to small changes in data when the grassy scenario applies.

This research presents a novel, enhanced model for Japanese term segmentation based on Extended Short-Term Memory. The original LSTM model struggles with accurately identifying certain Japanese terms due to its inflexible nature. In contrast, our proposed model overcomes this limitation and achieves improved results. The integration of additional lifetimes to LSTM, which enables multi-step data processing, significantly enhances the model's capabilities. The findings are supported by statistical significance, and experimental outcomes confirm the superior performance of this enhanced model.

External link sharing has been a longstanding issue on the Stack Overflow platform, leading to concerns over copyright infringement and potential violations of Stack Overflow's terms of service. Although internal link sharing within the community has been extensively studied, there remains a knowledge gap regarding external link sharing. This research aims to fill this knowledge gap by investigating the characteristics of external link sharing on Stack Overflow. A statistical analysis of 1,326,640 questions and their corresponding answers helped identify patterns in external link sharing, including the shared domains and their origins. Furthermore, the study examined the success rate of questions containing external links, as well as the impact of these links on question views and answer counts. Interestingly, the results showed that questions containing external links received more views and answers compared to those without such links. Nonetheless, the benefits of external link sharing were only evident when the links pointed to relevant and high-quality websites. This study's findings provide valuable insights for Stack Overflow moderators and the SO community to consider when deciding on external link sharing.

Galaxy diversity is a significant problem, more pronounced in training, as it distorts learning and reporting metrics, making findings less reliable. Numerous methods have been proposed to address this issue but, in the literature, there's a noticeable lack of comprehensive evaluations to determine their effectiveness. In this paper, we undertake a critical assessment of multiple techniques, including benchmarking them against each other and testing their responsiveness to varying problem characteristics. Our investigation employs a range of methods, including simulating different clustering densities and utilizing datasets from diverse real-world applications to construct a dataset suite. Key findings reveal that some techniques are highly adaptable, performing well in certain scenarios but poorly in others, while others show more consistent behavior although may require adjustment to achieve improved results. Our comparative analysis offers a clear distinction between the effectiveness of different methods, providing valuable insights that can inform the selection of the most suitable approach for a given task. Additionally, our evaluation identifies areas for improvement in each method, contributing to their development and fostering the research of galaxy variety mitigation strategies.

Establishing a comprehensive climate narrative is crucial for securing global climate change mitigation agreements, but it's hindered by the vast, dispersed nature of climate science research.  Although individual researchers and organizations extensively publish climate-related information, it remains inaccessible due to the numerous sources and varying topics.  A Climate Information Repository (CIR) addresses this issue by centralizing and structuring climate research for easy reference.  This paper outlines the objectives, design, and initial outcomes of the CIR in facilitating effective climate communication through a user-friendly interface.  The CIR's potential to enhance climate communication is demonstrated by a case study focusing on the importance of winter sea ice in Arctic climate change.  The CIR is an open-source, open-license platform for gathering, storing, and presenting climate information, which can be further developed by the climate science community to address other critical communication challenges.

Medical note transcription, including the extraction of sign events, has been a significant focus in the transcription industry. Currently, the transcription process is mainly done manually, but with the advancements in natural language processing, it has become a major area of study. The task of extracting sign events has been approached as a target detection task, where each target represents a critical medical event. A prominent dataset, MIMD, has been established for training and testing models in the extraction of target information from medical notes. It encompasses notes covering diverse topics, but primarily in the fields of surgery and obstetrics. In this research, we tackle the challenge of generalizing target information across different medical fields through the application of an object masking method. To achieve this, we propose an in-depth re-training protocol where a portion of the originally classified labels is concealed. The efficacy of our approach is demonstrated through experiments where models re-trained using our protocol surpass existing state-of-the-art methods.

The testing of Self-Driving Vehicles has escalated due to advancements in monocular perception and global mapping. However, the subject remains contentious due to the lack of transparent decision-making processes. In this context, we propose introducing Reinforcement Learning into the algorithmic framework of Self-Driving Vehicles to ensure safe navigation. By integrating Reinforcement Learning, which mimics human brain functionality by associating actions with consequences, the algorithm becomes more discerning and efficient in decision-making. We outline a novel approach, PRL-SDV, combining Reinforcement Learning with Deep Q-Networks, serving as a pioneering model for the autonomous vehicle's decision-making system. PRL-SDDV overcomes the limitations of conventional Autonomous Vehicles Technology by leveraging Reinforcement Learning for a more reasoning-driven approach. Furthermore, PRL-SDDV outperforms existing Autonomous Vehicle Technology in diverse scenarios, as evidenced by our simulation results.

In a binary neural network, the spiking-inhibitory perpendicular architecture achieves faster inference times and reduced energy consumption compared to traditional direct architecture. However, the latter's method of categorizing images by shifting them along the vertical axis can lead to inaccurate results in image recognition. A more efficient method has been devised to move in horizontal and vertical directions by simultaneously activating multiple neurons, and it has been given a mathematical explanation based on the characteristics of neural responses. This new method has been integrated into a random spiking neural network, and a new layer of vertical-inhibitory parallel architecture has been added to improve energy efficiency while maintaining accuracy. A pre-trained model is used to generate random weights for the network, and the horizontal shift is used to compensate for inaccuracies caused by misaligned pixel values. Experimental results show that this new approach compares favorably with other methods in both accuracy and energy consumption.

This research investigates the characteristics of a strange quark star at elevated temperatures, taking into consideration its spin alignment and a strong external magnetic field. The thermodynamic system is analyzed using the MIT bag model, and a detailed calculation of the star's mass, radius, and surface temperature is conducted across various temperature ranges. The findings reveal that a strange quark star's properties are substantially affected by temperature, but its spin alignment and magnetic field have distinct influences that vary with temperature.

A rapidly growing number of Internet users access content via their mobile devices, using a variety of operating systems and browsers. We have developed Pando, a novel volunteer computing system, which utilizes Internet access by these individuals to provide computational power on a large scale. Pando is specifically designed for use by individual volunteers and functions through a browser extension, operating independently of underlying system infrastructure. We describe a functional implementation of Pando and evaluate its security properties and advantages. We also report on our current deployment and showcase a practical application, using Pando to perform molecular simulations for drug research.

A temporal interpolation method called the minimal rational interpolation algorithm, independent of order, is used to estimate non-linear eigenvalues and modes in time series data. By incorporating a novel approach to construct observables, the frequency and hypercomplex properties of these eigenvalues can be confirmed. The accuracy of the estimation relies on correct order, a factor that can be influenced by measurement noise. A state-space model with a limited number of poles is created to simulate non-stationary signals and demonstrate the algorithm's capability on non-linearly oscillating systems, including a model representing a representative building and a gust-loaded cylinder system, both of which exhibit complex modes. Furthermore, the algorithm is tested on synthetic data from a reduced-order model and compared with results obtained using the multi-dimensional expectation-maximization algorithm. The findings show that the minimal rational interpolation algorithm can estimate non-linear eigenproperties with a higher level of accuracy than the EM algorithm.

In the framework of intermediate transitions being beta transfers with a specific energy gap, we seek to understand the nurturing environment for this process. Through a semi-classical and semi-classical+ argument, we investigate how the initial and final states' structural characteristics affect the transition rate. Notably, the transition rate is influenced by the overlap of wave functions in the initial and final states as well as the diameter of the transition zone. Additionally, by analyzing a specific model featuring a shell structure, we observe that intermediate transitions tend to occur between states with neighboring energy levels and similar spatial patterns, which enables us to generalize this behavior for both low and high transition energy across various nuclear states.

We've found that gauge theories with $SO(N_{c})$ as a gauge group and matter fields represented as vectors confine, resulting from monopole condensation and the quark bilinear breaking of chiral symmetry. Using an $SO(3)$ example, we demonstrate how this process occurs through an effective theory for defects, where a 't Hooft deformation of this theory forms an infrared fixed point that mirrors properties of the original $SO(3)$ theory. Moreover, in this context, we analyze the confinement and chiral symmetry breaking phases in theories with an additional $U(1)$ symmetry by examining various Dirac and Majorana masses for vector bilinears, which leads us to a novel phenomenon: mass deformation that breaks chiral symmetry without confining the fundamental fields.

Machine learning models like Random Forests have become widely accepted due to their robustness and ease of use, but the complexity of their structure limits understanding of individual predictions. We introduce a new method, Disentangled Assignment Curves, to clarify prediction processes in ensemble methods, focusing on Random Forests. Our tool generates a learned representation of each tree's structure, capturing the hierarchical relationships between nodes and observations. It then uses this representation to map trees to a common space, highlighting how trees change during classification. Our results show that DA Curves successfully interpret the predictions of both standalone and composite models, including Boosting algorithms. We also utilize DA Curves to enhance the performance of Machine Learning models, discovering optimal scenarios for using them in supervised learning. Additionally, we utilize our tool to rectify biases in datasets and uncover underlying patterns, such as date patterns in the Movielens dataset. Our tool is implemented in Python and can be accessed through our companion website.

A rapidly evolving AI scene, driven by the growing demand for AI-based decisions, is pushing the need for AI infrastructure to be both secure and efficient.  Despite significant advancements in mini-computers and AI processors, security risks persist, necessitating accelerated innovations.  Recent breakthroughs in secure virtualization, trusted execution environments, and post-quantum cryptography create opportunities for new solutions.  We propose an innovative model for collaborative AI training, combining the efficiency of shared computing and secure data protection using TEEs.  Our new framework enables multiple organizations to jointly train neural networks while safeguarding their data within separate TEEs.  We introduce a novel concept of "trusted prefixes" to split model layers into compute and trainable layers, and a specialized communication mechanism for data exchange through TEEs.  Our proof-of-concept implementation using MambaK and PyTorch demonstrates the efficiency and security of this approach, with significant compute overhead and minor friction losses.  We discuss the potential for our model to meet emerging standards in the emerging AI infrastructure market.

A key challenge in assessing human performance via robotic systems revolves around achieving precise and accurate measurements of operator abilities. When traditional methods are employed, several complications arise, including large equipment footprints and stringent safety requirements. To overcome these issues, this research introduces an innovative approach to evaluating human performance using a fully automated, portable system. By combining the capabilities of target tracking and hand movement analysis, our solution estimates and calculates human accuracy with remarkable efficiency. To date, several promising results have been achieved with successful tracking trials conducted both indoors and outdoors using low-cost, deeply integrated sensors, and a compact robotic platform as the target.

Advancements in service deployment technologies have enabled the construction of sophisticated, distributed systems from individual microservices, which can be proactively protected by automated clustering of these services. To enhance security in such environments, individual microservices are grouped into containers, each isolated from others, allowing for efficient monitoring and management of large distributed systems. However, the inherent isolation of containers hinders communication between microservices, requiring the employment of reusable proxies to facilitate smooth interaction between clustered containers. To effectively intercept malicious requests at this level, a next-generation filtering system is needed that can learn and adapt to the intricate behaviors of microservices on the fly, integrating knowledge from both container clustering and artificial intelligence. A promising approach to achieving this goal involves training a flow-based proxy using neural networks to identify and categorize service patterns, enabling more sophisticated anomaly detection in complex distributed systems. A recent neural network-based microservice training system known as FlowGAN can effectively classify service patterns, but suffers from poor performance in systems featuring unexpected variations, limiting its effectiveness in highly dynamic environments. To address these limitations, a novel training system called Timeloops is proposed, designed to learn adaptive patterns in dynamic microservice environments. Timeloops combines elements of container clustering and machine learning to produce a scalable flow proxy, capable of identifying service patterns even in the most challenging context. By integrating the capabilities of a container monitor and a neural network, Timeloops trains a proxy to automatically recognize and respond to microservices, effectively filtering malicious requests and enhancing the security

Linear classifiers have become widely-used models in numerous applications across computer science and social sciences. Our research explores how linear classifiers behave in a complex dataset consisting of interconnected items with varying densities. To enhance understanding, we create a stylized model, focusing on distribution shapes and analysis, to better comprehend the effects of dataset structures on linear classifier models. Our findings reveal that when linear classifiers are trained on this complex dataset, they tend to discriminate between densely and sparsely populated areas. Additionally, we observed that linear classifiers can distinguish between different data patterns, such as clusters, chains, and tree-like structures. Our research also investigates how these shapes influence the performance and interpretability of linear classifiers, highlighting that certain shapes result in more predictable and transparent model outcomes.

The stellar dynamics around a supermassive black hole in a galaxy core can provide valuable insights into the star cluster formation processes influenced by the black hole. We have established a general approach to study this region using a collisionless framework. By combining the cluster Arrangements framework, we observe the stellar distribution, originating from a finite number of discrete star clusters, based on their radial positions and gravitational binding energies. The Arrangements framework reveals how a galaxy core's stellar distribution evolves from initially grouped star clusters dispersed by orbital mixing processes. We apply the framework to simulate various initial cluster distributions, ranging from tight groups to loosely bound stellar coalesces, around a $3 \times 10^9 \M_\odot$ supermassive black hole with a central density of $10^6 \M_\odot \, \text{pc}^{-2}$. The simulated group properties in our model align with real-world observations of stellar groups in galaxy cores. We find a significant influence of the initial cluster distribution on the orbital eccentricities of the groups and their radial positions. Conversely, group properties are largely unaffected by the black hole's gravitational influence within a limited radius. Ultimately, the Arrangements framework provides a comprehensive tool to study the various stellar group stages in a galaxy core, offering a potential explanation for the origin of the observed centrally peaked stars in galaxy cores.

We've explored a complex system consisting of two interconnected power generators, a load, and a power distribution system, all controlled by a power management system trying to maintain stable voltage across the network. This control system uses a simplified thermal model, neglecting dynamic responses, which are unimportant due to the rapid communication feedback time. However, the system's slow mechanical response requires consideration. The power management system, modeled as a controllable power source, seeks to regulate the network's active and reactive power while meeting generator output constraints, despite variable generator efficiencies and heat transfer limitations. To achieve stable voltage, the power management system uses predictive control, regulating both active and reactive power in real-time. But, due to communication delays, the power management system uses a predictive control approach, generating a steady-state power output forecasted at a shorter time interval. This control strategy faces a challenge: it's hard to reach a power output adjustment soon after receiving updated information, which leads to oscillating system behavior. To address this issue, the power management system implements a model predictive control tactic, altering the power output within a specified boundary after each oscillation cycle. By adjusting the model predictive control boundary, the power management system can enhance system performance, which is verified through an indirect model, despite unknown generator dynamics.

Deep learning's significant success across various domains can be attributed to the relentless pursuit of efficiency, specifically in terms of computational efficiency and learning efficiency. The emergence of differentiable separation methods, such as Independent Component Analysis (ICA) and Unsupervised Component Analysis (UCA), offers a new approach to efficiently learn low-dimensional representations directly from data, surpassing traditional models' limitations. Building upon this idea, we introduce a new algorithm, Compressive UCA, which enables learning low-dimensional representations while reducing the dimensionality of the representations themselves, resulting in improved computational efficiency. We further develop a comprehensive theoretical framework, which enables the design of new and flexible variants of Compressive UCA. We then establish the effectiveness of our proposed method through thorough experimental evaluations on multiple datasets.

We introduce and investigate a voter model that incorporates both competitive and colonizing characteristics in an effort to understand how multiple species interact and evolve within an ecosystem. This model builds upon the traditional voter model by incorporating a competition-colonization mechanism, thereby creating a dynamical system that is capable of exhibiting chaotic behavior. We have determined that this model possesses a unique coexistence equilibrium that can be described mathematically, and we have developed conditions to identify whether this equilibrium is either stable or unstable. Furthermore, we have developed a metric to calculate the likelihood of an invading species establishing a foothold in an ecosystem previously inhabited by a dominant species. Through various numerical simulations, we have confirmed our theoretical findings and observed that the model's behavior can transition from a diverse, chaotic state to a uniform state where one species dominates. Conversely, from a uniform state, the model can exhibit a range of diverse outcomes.

In the context of the abelian quantum dual model, we develop a concept of subregionally extended unitary equivalence within von Neumann algebras, which forms a category that contains unitary morphisms. We demonstrate that unitary equivalence within a given algebra is completely defined by the topology of its constituent unitary morphisms. Furthermore, unitary morphism compositions serve as the fundamental means of establishing equivalence relationships. Notably, the ambient space in which states reside plays an insignificant role in this equivalence. We find that the category consisting of subregionally extended unitary equivalence von Neumann algebras and their associated morphisms exhibits properties resembling path algebra behavior.

To improve magnon-photon-phonon entanglement in a chamber magnomechanics system, we have enhanced the technique by incorporating coherent feedback. In the optimized setup, a Tavis-Cummings model interacts with a discrete driving field, a bath for thermal phonons, and a mesoscopic capacitor coupled to a bulk magnetic resonator. The input from an external driving field mixes magnons and photons in the system. We have found that when the system is in a specific steady-state, the desired entanglement can be optimized through parameter adjustments. The outcome shows that coherent feedback significantly enhances the entanglement capacity of the system, surpassing what could be achieved without this feedback. Furthermore, we have found that in the optimized setup, the steady-state magnon-photon-photon tripartite correlation is nearly perfect, while the magnon-photon-photon bipartite correlation approaches its maximum possible value of one. The outcome also indicates that the magnon-photon-photon tripartite correlation is highly resilient to thermal phonons, making the optimized setup an ideal platform for applications requiring robust tripartite correlations.

We provide a detailed single-particle insertion of color-sensitive elements in the anomalous dimension of the triple-collinear operator, maintaining $D$-dimensional integrity and using an $ \epsilon $-regulated self-energy and soft functions to obtain results in both space- and momentum-space representations. Our work is specifically tailored for applications in massively-spaced-out scenarios, such as numerical particle physics simulations, and we provide a publicly accessible code with this paper for quick retrieval of our findings.
A formal proof for the Neron Desingularization, a multidimensional case algorithm, has been formulated for one-dimensional local domains, and it's been implemented in the software package Singular.

Ancient sundials held significant cultural importance in understanding historical timelines and astronomical knowledge. The process of transversal sunlight through the shadow of a gnomon enabled premodern societies to determine local time, evaluate solar movement, and calculate seasonal changes. Theoretical models for sundial design have been documented in historical texts but actual physical examples provide first-hand evidence of craftsmanship and the cultural values of their creators. This research aims to document the process of building and utilizing a classic Latin-style sundial in Indonesia. By following established protocols for creating Latin-style sundials, we can gain insight into the skills of modern Indonesian craftsmen and highlight the connection between classic designs and innovative innovations in sundial replication. Additionally, by studying this sundial's functionality, we can demonstrate its effectiveness in determining local time and evaluating solar movement in Indonesia.

A revolutionary 6G surface-to-air communication technology has been proposed, which enables devices to communicate with each other directly while coexisting with conventional IP traffic over the same surface. To address the complex challenge of managing both power consumption and data traffic on the surface, a new fully integrated network architecture is proposed, where power and data signals are combined into a single intelligence reflector surface. As a result, significant reductions in power consumption and enhanced data communication capabilities can be achieved. To optimize this new integrated network, a deep learning-based surface-assisted integrated data and power networking (SIDPN) scheme is proposed, which utilizes neural networks trained with deep Q-learning to develop an SIDPN surface-assisted power control (SSPC) algorithm. To evaluate the performance of this new integration, a general energy efficiency (GE) metric is proposed, which demonstrates the ability of the trained neural network to generate optimal training sequences for the SSPC algorithm, leading to higher GE values. Furthermore, the deepest neural network is explored, which utilizes its last layer to generate orthogonal power beams for each device, while the reflector surface forms orthogonal data channels. This new integration offers improved power efficiency and data communication capabilities, outperforming conventional 5G networks in terms of energy efficiency.

A cutting-edge innovation in LDV technology has reached a breakthrough in its potential to transform the field of experimental research. A highly advanced computer-controlled LDV system has been developed, enabling the conversion of a traditional single-point LDV system into a sophisticated imaging system. This ground-breaking technology facilitates the acquisition of two-dimensional velocity measurements, representing a significant breakthrough in LDV advancements. The newly integrated system empowers researchers to obtain detailed three-dimensional velocity patterns, even in complex flow setups with intricate geometries, beyond the capabilities of traditional single-point measurements. The impressive data acquisition rate of up to 50,000 measurements per second allows for the analysis of highly turbulent flows, including intricate spatial patterns and rapid velocity fluctuations. The system's capabilities are exemplified through the measurement and detailed visualization of turbulent flow patterns in a circular pipe.

In category theory, especially when working with topos theory, binary relations play a crucial role as the foundation for categorical abstraction of point-free ring theory. This commentary examines the concept of spectra of ideals within commutative rings, establishing a connection to binary relations as their primary categorical representation. This involves exploring the correspondence between spectra and binary relations, including the construction of the functor that maps rings to their corresponding spectra. This functor is shown to be faithful but not full, with the exception of a specific subset of binary relations known as diagonal relations. These results have significant implications for the study of classical first-order logic in the context of spectrums, suggesting that certain model-theoretic concepts can be extended to the extended real line and its subsets, even in the absence of a topological structure. This involves establishing a connection between binary relations and the collection of extended real intervals, including their closure under finite unions and intersections. Furthermore, a binary relation is shown to define a continuous valuation on the collection of rational intervals if and only if it is diagonal. This involves exploring the relationship between binary relations and continuous valuations as opposite categories.

To investigate the feasibility of utilizing a programmable phase disk within a transmission electron microscope (TEM), we conducted an experiment where a square pattern of 10 by 10 resolution was projected onto a microscope using the programmable disk, with the resolution verified through a nearby camera capturing an image of the diffraction pattern. Furthermore, we demonstrated that by shifting this projected pattern it is possible to obtain images of specimens at resolutions higher than those achievable with the microscope alone, with multiple specimens able to be captured within a single area, and an improvement in resolution attainable well beyond the capabilities of the microscope itself.

In 1918, Richard Courant published a report on assessment methods for the Prussian mathematical Olympiad.
